The potential areas for cooperation are quite concrete: common transit tariffs, digital customs procedures, coordinated port and railway schedules, joint investment funds, green energy exports, tourism routes and coordination at international forums. With its ports, financial resources and transport links through the Caucasus and Turkey, Azerbaijan offers Central Asian countries additional routes and opportunities. Baku, in turn, gains more systematic access to the region’s five markets and their economic ties with China.

However, there are also many constraints. The six countries differ in their economic potential, interests in water resources and energy, and priorities in their relations with Russia, China, Turkey and the West. The format has no permanent secretariat or mechanisms to enforce decisions, so implementation of political agreements will depend on intergovernmental coordination.

The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, has yet to be ratified by Iran, while delimiting the seabed requires separate agreements. Falling water levels in the Caspian, the shallowing of ports and the need for costly dredging also increase the environmental and economic costs of transport logistics.

From symbol to concrete projects?

Mirziyoyev has already proposed transforming the format into a “Community of Central Asia” with a rotating secretariat. The next official meeting, scheduled for 8 October 2026 in Avaza, will be one of the first tests of whether these intentions can turn into practical decisions.

Will the six countries agree on common tariffs, digital customs procedures and a stable ferry schedule? Will TRIPP become a fully fledged part of the Middle Corridor without creating new border disputes? Or will the “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format remain a flexible consultative platform, with its informal nature continuing to be its main advantage?

Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

World.title: Convicted former Georgian PM Garibashvili: ‘Authorities left me no choice, I have to fight’
World.content:
Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

Convicted former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili says in a letter published from prison that the authorities arrested him to end his political career. He also says he gave up his legal fight to avoid a confrontation with the authorities.

The former prime minister writes that he received a letter from Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. According to Garibashvili, he confirmed to Mdinaradze that same day that he did not intend to return to politics.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s press office has described Garibashvili’s claims as “complete absurdity”.

“I state with full responsibility that I did everything to avoid confrontation with the [ruling] team and with someone who is dear to me,” Garibashvili wrote.

He says this is why he abandoned his legal challenge and went through the entire process to the end — to avoid, as he put it, harming the interests of the state and the “team”.

“Unfortunately, in response I received a staged dirty provocation, a sea of lies and injustice. Throughout this time, the public heard not a single word from me. I endured this ordeal patiently,” Garibashvili said.

According to Garibashvili, despite the position he had expressed to Mdinaradze, the authorities believed there was still a “1% risk” that he might return to politics in the future.

“To avoid this, they wanted me to face corruption charges and admit guilt,” Garibashvili writes.

According to him, this demand became a “red line” that forced him to take the “most difficult step of my life” — to turn against the authorities.

“I have no other choice. I am forced to start fighting,” the former prime minister said.

On 17 August 2026, Garibashvili made his first public statement from prison. In a Facebook post, he said he had received an ultimatum in a letter sent on the instructions of Bidzina Ivanishvili. He added that he had “no other choice” but to stand against what he described as “evil that insults my dignity”.

“I tried to do everything possible to avoid taking this step, but unfortunately I have no other choice but to confront this evil that insults my dignity. I must confront this ruthless cruelty, oppression and injustice, as well as the dirty plan to destroy me and my family,” Garibashvili wrote.

He also said that Bidzina Ivanishvili and the government bear responsibility for the safety of both himself and his family.

In the letter, Garibashvili says he had remained publicly silent and patiently endured what was happening until now. However, he says the current situation has left him no choice but to begin fighting.

Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

World.title: Armenian prime minister’s wife launches campaign against domestic violence
World.content:
Anna Hakobyan’s campaign against domestic violence

The wife of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Anna Hakobyan, has announced the launch of a campaign against domestic violence. She received death threats shortly after calling for a public discussion of the issue. However, she continues to actively promote her initiative.

“The first stage will involve drafting comprehensive and effective legislation and discussing it in the National Assembly,” she said.

According to Anna Hakobyan, the Criminal Code should define domestic violence separately as “a distinct and independent crime”. She plans to invite female MPs from the parliament’s two opposition factions to join her initiative. If they do, she believes there is a chance that “parliament will unanimously approve the bill”.

Anna Hakobyan calls for a “family model with no place for violence”

The prime minister’s wife posted a video message on social media in which she said she intended to continue fighting domestic violence. According to Hakobyan, Armenia’s traditional family model, which hides various forms of violence, should give way to a model of a “family with no place for violence, based on mutual love and respect”. She proposes amending the Criminal Code to achieve this goal:

“An individual article should be added to the Code to establish criminal liability for all forms of domestic violence. Alternatively, different chapters of the Code could include provisions covering specific forms of domestic violence, including beatings, psychological abuse, economic abuse, bodily harm, sexual violence and others.”

According to Anna Hakobyan, eradicating violence requires clear, realistic and effective legal mechanisms.

Before presenting the bill to parliament, she initiated discussions with independent experts and female MPs. Together, they plan to examine gaps in the existing legislation. Once the law comes into force, she has promised to launch the initiative’s second stage. This will involve:

organising an awareness campaign;

improving the skills of staff at relevant agencies;

ensuring the effective implementation of the new regulations.

“At the same time, a group of respected experts is preparing a nationwide study to collect the most accurate and comprehensive data possible on the prevalence of domestic violence against women in Armenia,” she said.

What preceded the campaign

This is not the prime minister’s wife’s first post about domestic violence. She has been actively raising the issue on her social media pages. At the end of July, she said she had received threats after a particular post, including threats to kill her.

“I hope the state authorities can prevent such a development, as it would seriously damage the country’s reputation if the prime minister’s wife became a victim of violence,” Hakobyan said.

At the same time, she urged women to overcome their fears and report cases of violence.

The Prosecutor General’s Office took note of her report. The Investigative Committee said it had opened a criminal case under the article on “hooliganism using information and communication technologies”.

“In addition, within the framework of another criminal case concerning public calls for violence, a warrant has been issued for the arrest of one person. The person has been placed on the wanted list,” Investigative Committee spokeswoman Kim Avdalyan said.

Statistics on domestic violence

The Investigative Committee said it opened 1,794 criminal cases related to domestic violence in the first half of 2026:

712 cases carried over from 2025;

1,082 cases opened in 2026.

Authorities sent 204 criminal cases to court and charged 213 people.

Of the 213 defendants in the cases sent to court, 150 were spouses of the victims, 20 were partners, 15 were parents or grandparents, five were brothers or sisters, 16 were children or grandchildren, one was the husband’s sister or brother, and six were sons- or daughters-in-law.

Of the 213 victims, 192 were over 18, while the rest were minors. Of those, 13 were under 12, three were aged 13-14, and five were aged 15-18.

Anna Hakobyan’s campaign against domestic violence

World.title: ‘Work is being carried out to international standards’ — Georgia’s Gelati Monastery Rehabilitation Committee responds to criticism
World.content:
Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati has described reports circulating on social media and in the media about conservation work at the monastery as disinformation.

The committee said the disinformation was harming efforts to restore Gelati.

The Gelati Monastery complex is one of Georgia’s most important medieval cultural and religious monuments. King David IV, known as David the Builder, founded it in 1106.

The complex’s main church is the Cathedral of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary. In medieval Georgia, Gelati was not only a monastery but also an important centre of education and scholarship, home to the renowned Gelati Academy.

Recent reports and assessments have raised concerns about the condition of Gelati. The debate has focused on several issues:

The church’s temporary roof, which critics have called “cellophane”;

The risk of frescoes collapsing;

Mould and condensation inside the church;

The condition of the drainage system;

Plans to install an underfloor heating system;

Cooperation with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure;

The condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

What does the committee say?

The committee rejects claims that the Gelati Cathedral is covered with “cellophane”. According to the committee, the creation of a single temporary covering for the cathedral was one of the main requirements set by the UNESCO World Heritage Centre as early as 2020.

The committee says Georgian and German specialists jointly designed the roof. The authorities approved the project after considering several proposals. The covering uses a high-tech PVC-based material made in Germany specifically for Gelati. According to the committee, the material meets international conservation standards.

The committee also rejects reports of widespread loss of frescoes inside the cathedral. It says all critically damaged areas have been stabilised, while conservation work on the wall paintings is continuing in stages.

The statement also addresses Gelati’s historic drainage system. According to the committee, drainage channels built during the reign of David the Builder stopped functioning in 1510 after Ottoman forces burned the monastery. The committee says archaeological excavations also support this conclusion.

“For centuries, the drainage system was filled with earth, ash and coal,” the committee said.

The committee also responded to criticism over humidity and condensation inside the church. According to the committee, Italian professor Dario Camuffo conducted the study of Gelati’s microclimate. The committee considers him one of the recognised experts in the study of the microclimate of cultural heritage sites.

The committee explained that the problem at Gelati stems from the church’s massive walls, which retain the cold for a long time during winter. In spring, when outdoor temperatures rise and warm air enters the church, condensation can form on the walls and floor.

Camuffo suggested gradually heating the floor as one possible solution. However, the committee stressed that this remains a working hypothesis and requires further research before a final decision.

The committee also clarified the memorandum it signed with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure. According to the committee, the “pilot restoration” provided for in the document does not mean conducting experiments at Gelati. Instead, it refers to pilot or trial restoration work, which is standard international practice.

“This is a widely accepted standard for restoring wall paintings. Before treating an entire fresco, conservators test the safety of the proposed conservation methods on a small, less visible area. Only after obtaining a positive result do they begin the full-scale process,” the committee said.

In a significant part of its statement, the committee also responded to critics and addressed allegations about the condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

According to the committee, experts already knew about the poor condition of the mosaics in 1989. The claim is based on an assessment by restorer Carlo Bakuradze at the time, who found that about 85% of the mosaic depicting the Virgin Mary had detached from its base.

The committee also criticised specialists who question the ongoing conservation work and reminded them of their own responsibility for Gelati’s condition in the past.

“It is cynical and hypocritical for people to question the quality of conservation work when, under their direct supervision, extensive water-infiltration problems emerged within just one year at the recently built Bagrati Cathedral — problems that persist to this day,” the statement said. The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati urged critics not to try to damage the reputation of the ongoing work and to act according to professional ethics.

“We call on those pursuing certain subjective goals and agendas to refrain from attempts to discredit the conservation work carried out under the Gelati rehabilitation programme and deliberately mislead the public. We also call on them to return to the standards of common decency and professional ethics,” the committee said.

The committee concluded by stressing again that the work at the Gelati Monastery complex is unprecedented in scale, involves international experts and meets international conservation standards.

What happened at Gelati?

The main problem at Gelati Monastery is water and dampness, which have damaged the church’s wall paintings and mosaics over time. The situation became particularly serious after restoration work in recent years, including problems with the roof.

The problem became so serious that the UNESCO World Heritage Centre and its advisory bodies issued specific recommendations to Georgia. The authorities changed their approach to the restoration work in response to those recommendations and established the current Rehabilitation Committee.

A ruling by Georgia’s Supreme Court also notes that workers carried out roofing work at Gelati without an adequate expert assessment. The court found that problems with the materials used and the quality of the installation created a real risk of water entering the building.

Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

World.title: Suicides in Armenia’s military: the statistics and debate over who should be held responsible
World.content:
Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

In Armenia, debate continues over the causes of military deaths in peacetime and who should bear responsibility. A series of suicides has prompted the latest discussions. The first incident occurred on 21 July. Then, on 13 August, the Defence Ministry reported that it had found the body of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan with a gunshot wound. In both cases, the Investigative Committee said it had opened criminal proceedings under the article on negligent incitement to suicide.

According to the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, this was the 31st military death in Armenia in 2026. However, the Defence Ministry says 11 servicemen have died. Moreover, the ministry’s spokesperson said the number of military deaths had become the subject of various forms of manipulation.

“We often see reports in the press about 30 deaths in the army over the course of a year. But no one says how many of those 30 cases actually occurred in the army, which were related to military service and which were not. Even if the deaths were related to service, were all of them murders and suicides?” Aram Torosyan said, calling for greater precision.

Government bodies and civil society organisations also differ over who should bear responsibility for military deaths. Human rights groups tend to argue that the defence minister and the chief of the General Staff should be held accountable. However, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan does not share this view.

“In my assessment, it is not the case that the chief of the General Staff and the defence minister are failing to make sufficient efforts to address this issue,” Nikol Pashinyan said.

Civil society data differs from official figures

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan, who represents the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, said she had seen no positive changes. According to her, the number of military deaths in non-combat situations has not decreased:

“The situation is even worse than in 2025. There were 35 deaths throughout 2025, while there have already been 31 cases in the first eight months of this year.”

She stressed that 10 cases in 2025 were classified as related to military service, while the same number have been recorded in just eight months this year.

Defence Ministry spokesman Aram Torosyan says these claims do not match the official statistics.

“We have recorded 11 deaths this year. Only five of those who died were serving their mandatory military service. Some died from illness, while others died in a mine explosion,” he said.

Torosyan said six of the 11 deaths involved suicide or incitement to suicide, but only three were related to military service.

Commenting on last year’s figures, he stressed that there were no cases of murder in the army in 2025.

Causes of suicides in the army

The authorities have not released details about the death of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan. However, the prime minister said that 85-90% of suicides in the army result from:

gambling addiction and the debts it causes;

personal and family problems;

servicemen falling asleep while on duty, which can lead to conflicts with fellow soldiers.

“If a serviceman on duty at a border post falls asleep, he puts other people’s lives at risk. Soldiers then begin to treat the person who fell asleep at the post negatively, and he becomes isolated. After returning from combat duty, psychological pressure can also follow. We should not place all the blame on the army leadership. I am responsible for the fact that we have still not found a solution to this problem,” Pashinyan said.

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan believes that the first two causes mentioned by the prime minister have nothing to do with the army. At the same time, she believes authorities can eliminate the third factor by taking systemic measures:

“Why does a serviceman fall asleep while on duty? Are there enough personnel to ensure that everyone gets enough rest and does not feel the need to sleep while on duty?”

Prime minister’s statements and dismissals

On the day the soldier died, Nikol Pashinyan told reporters that the government had discussed the situation and decided to make dismissals. He announced personnel changes in the Military Police and the Defence Ministry’s Department of Moral and Psychological Support:

“We will analyse in detail why our efforts in this area are not producing the desired results and draw conclusions. Yes, there must be individual accountability.”

The same day, reports emerged that Military Police chief Ashot Zakaryan had submitted his resignation. Today, the president dismissed Zakaryan from the post he had held for six years. In another decree, Major General Aram Hovhannisyan was appointed to replace him. From 2023 to 2025, he served as deputy interior minister and police chief.

There are no specific details yet about personnel changes in the Department of Moral and Psychological Support.

In recent days, the Defence Ministry has reported consultations on organising psychological support in the armed forces. To review a report on the psychological assistance provided to the military, the defence minister met professors from Yerevan State University’s Research Centre for Psychology. The ministry is also holding discussions with conscript sergeants and officers serving on duty at military posts.

“The agenda includes issues related to preventing hazing and eliminating inappropriate behaviour in the army,” the ministry said.

Comment

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan believes:

“The army’s top command, led by Suren Papikyan, must give the public a detailed explanation of the series of deaths.

Has anyone from the army’s top command visited the military unit to establish the circumstances of the soldier’s death and find out what was happening there? I strongly doubt it.

Papikyan did not even visit the military unit in the village of Azat when 15 servicemen died.

On 19 January 2023, a fire broke out in the engineering and sapper company’s premises in the village of Azat, killing 15 servicemen. Three others suffered burns of varying severity.

Then, as now, Nikol Pashinyan spoke on Papikyan’s behalf. He named those responsible and accountable. But he did not explain what the Military Police had to do with the death.

If Pashinyan knows more about the situation in the army and at military units, why is Papikyan still the defence minister?”

Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

World.title: White House: China is using Georgia to circumvent US tariffs
World.content:
US tariffs on China

According to a White House report titled The Great Transshipment Scam, China is using third countries, including Georgia, to circumvent US tariffs.

The Trump administration’s report names 40 countries and territories as participants in China’s “shadow shipping network”. The White House says these countries may have helped China circumvent US trade restrictions by transshipping and processing goods destined for the US.

The report divides the economies into three categories:

The first category includes countries and trading blocs that receive significant volumes of China-linked goods but have diversified industrial markets. The White House places Canada, the European Union, India, Israel, Japan, Mexico, South Korea and Taiwan in this group.

The second category includes countries with significant economic integration with China. According to the report, these are Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Turkey and Vietnam.

The third category includes China’s “secondary targets”. The White House considers this group to include relatively small economies such as Georgia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Argentina, Switzerland, Panama, Colombia, Chile, Cambodia and the United Arab Emirates.

According to the report, rerouting Chinese goods through third countries is one of the mechanisms companies use to avoid US tariffs on Chinese imports.

The White House published the report as part of the broader trade policy of the US administration. One of its main goals is to tighten enforcement of restrictions on imports from China and prevent companies from circumventing tariffs through third countries.

In 2025, Georgia imported $1.98 billion worth of goods from China, while its exports to the US amounted to just $120 million.

The value of goods imported from China into Georgia was significantly higher than the value of Georgian exports to the US. According to 2025 data, ferroalloys accounted for the largest category of goods imported from China into Georgia.

During the same period, Georgia’s main exports to the US included power-generating equipment and passenger cars.

Trade data show that Chinese imports account for a significant share of Georgia’s trade with China, while Georgian exports to the US remain relatively small.

US President Donald Trump began imposing and gradually increasing tariffs on Chinese goods in February 2025. By April 2025, the rate had reached 145%. Beijing responded with similar measures, imposing a 125% tariff on US products.

Following talks in May that year, the US cut the newly imposed tariffs from 145% to 30%, while China reduced its tariffs from 125% to 10%. However, other tariffs introduced before 2025 remained in place.

According to data published by the US Congress, various tariffs on Chinese goods are currently in effect under several US laws. Some target China directly, while others apply to specific economic sectors and also affect Chinese goods.

US tariffs on China

World.title: Deportation, ‘international wanted list’ mark new escalation in Baku-Moscow tensions
World.content:
Escalation in Azerbaijani-Russian relations

Two developments on 17 August highlighted the continuing fragility of relations between Baku and Moscow. Russia deported Bakhtiyar Hasanov, chairman of the Azerbaijani National-Cultural Autonomy in Moscow, to Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan, in turn, placed three Russian citizens on an international wanted list: Moscow 24 TV presenter Ivan Knyazev, political consultant and media expert Semyon Uralov, and journalist and adviser to the Russian transport minister Alexei Chadayev.

The fact that the two developments occurred on the same day may at first suggest that they were reciprocal measures. However, the process that culminated in Hasanov’s deportation had begun well before 17 August, with his case under consideration for at least several months. Therefore, while there is no public evidence of a direct causal link between the two decisions, both developments fit into the broader pattern of the prolonged deterioration in Azerbaijani-Russian relations.

Deportation of Bakhtiyar Hasanov

According to open sources, Bakhtiyar Hasanov was detained in Russia in June 2026 and placed in a temporary detention centre for foreign nationals. He appealed against the decision to deport him, but the court rejected his appeal.

According to sources, Hasanov’s Russian citizenship was revoked in September 2025. In autumn 2025, the Agentstvo media outlet established that Hasanov’s passport, issued in 2019, was listed as invalid in a Russian government database. Hasanov himself denied at the time that he had been stripped of his citizenship.

One of the key questions is the legal basis on which his citizenship was revoked. Open sources provide no complete or unequivocal explanation for the decision.

The case also carries political significance because of Hasanov’s status. For many years, he cooperated with official Moscow bodies dealing with diaspora and interethnic relations and served on public councils. His deportation is therefore also being viewed as part of a broader trend of pressure on the Azerbaijani diaspora in Russia.

Growing pressure on the diaspora

Since the summer of 2025, several prominent members of the Azerbaijani diaspora in Russia have been stripped of their citizenship, detained or expelled from the country. The names of Arshad Khankishiyev, Elshan Ibrahimov and Javid Rzayev have been mentioned in this context.

Russian nationalist and Kremlin-aligned media have largely portrayed these measures as part of efforts to combat illegal migration, alleged links to criminal groups and security concerns. However, final court rulings on all the allegations made against these individuals are not publicly available.

This process took on a more overtly political dimension following an operation targeting Azerbaijani families in Yekaterinburg in June 2025. The deaths of the Safarov brothers during the operation prompted a sharp reaction from Baku. Moscow linked the operation to an investigation into crimes committed many years earlier, while the Azerbaijani side focused on reports of violence and torture against those detained.

Since then, the issue of the diaspora has gradually moved beyond the social and cultural sphere and become one of the instruments of political pressure in relations between the two countries.

Baku’s charges against three Russian citizens

On 17 August, Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office said that Ivan Knyazev, Semyon Uralov and Alexei Chadayev had been placed on a wanted list as part of a criminal investigation.

The investigation relates to programmes published on Uralov’s YouTube channel on 14 July and 13 August. According to the Azerbaijani authorities, the broadcasts contained calls for the violent overthrow of the country’s constitutional order, violations of its territorial integrity, terrorist activity and incitement of ethnic hatred.

The criminal case is being investigated under Articles 214-2, 281.2 and 283.2.1 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code. A court ordered the three men to be detained in absentia.

Excerpts from the broadcasts published by Azerbaijani media include remarks about a possible military operation against Baku, military pressure on Azerbaijan from the Caspian Sea and the use of physical violence against the country’s leadership. However, the Prosecutor General’s Office has not published full transcripts of the broadcasts, expert assessments or all the episodes on which the charges are based.

What do Uralov and Chadayev say?

The accused reject Baku’s allegations. Alexei Chadayev denied inciting ethnic hatred, saying that his criticism was directed not against the Azerbaijani people but against the country’s political leadership.

Semyon Uralov, for his part, described the Azerbaijani authorities’ decision as politically motivated. In subsequent Telegram posts, he continued to sharply criticise the political systems of post-Soviet countries, including the Azerbaijani authorities.

The response indicates that the case has moved beyond the legal sphere and become part of the broader information confrontation between the two countries.

‘International wanted list’ does not mean automatic arrest

The term “international wanted list”, used by Azerbaijani media, does not mean that a wanted person will automatically be arrested in another country.

Even if Interpol issues a Red Notice, it does not constitute an international arrest warrant. Each country decides whether to detain a wanted person in accordance with its own laws. In addition, Interpol’s constitution prohibits the organisation from intervening in matters of a political, military, religious or racial character.

The outcome of Baku’s request will therefore depend on the legal evidence submitted, as well as on how other countries assess the case — as a criminal prosecution or as a continuation of the political confrontation.

Ukraine factor

The latest escalation in Azerbaijani-Russian relations comes against the backdrop of the growing prominence of the Ukraine issue.

On 6 August, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov made his first official visit to Kyiv since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and visited Irpin. Azerbaijan reiterated its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders. The two sides also discussed the possibility of supplying Azerbaijani gas to Ukraine.

Against this political backdrop, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko visited Baku on 16–17 August and met Ilham Aliyev. The presentation to Aliyev of a certificate naming him an honorary citizen of Irpin could be perceived in Moscow as a symbolic political gesture.

There is no evidence confirming a direct link between these developments and Hasanov’s deportation. However, the Azerbaijani leadership’s increasingly open articulation of a position on Ukraine that differs from Moscow’s fits into the broader picture of growing discontent in Russian political circles.

New mechanisms of mutual pressure

One notable change in relations between Baku and Moscow over the past two years has been the increasingly active use of law-enforcement and administrative mechanisms in the context of their political confrontation.

Russia has applied citizenship and migration laws, as well as criminal legislation, against members of the Azerbaijani diaspora. Azerbaijan, in turn, has used criminal prosecution mechanisms against individuals linked to Russian media over statements that Baku regards as posing a threat to the country.

This does not in itself mean that the legal arguments put forward by either side are unfounded. However, the fact that such legal measures are being taken against the backdrop of political crises in bilateral relations inevitably raises questions about their selective application and possible use for political purposes.

Where are relations heading?

At this stage, a complete political rupture between Azerbaijan and Russia appears unlikely. The two countries have significant mutual interests in areas including trade, transport, logistics and regional security.

At the same time, a return to the previous level of relations also appears difficult. Instead, an emerging model seems to be characterised by political mistrust alongside continued, limited cooperation.

Azerbaijanis living in Russia, as well as diaspora organisations maintaining social ties between the two countries, could find themselves particularly vulnerable in this confrontation. The use of diaspora representatives as instruments in an interstate dispute, particularly when accompanied by ethnic rhetoric, increases the risk that tensions could extend beyond diplomatic relations and affect relations between the two societies.

The events of 17 August therefore have broader significance than two separate legal decisions. They point to the emergence of a new model of relations in which Baku and Moscow, while continuing to cooperate, are increasingly making use of political and legal means to exert pressure on one another.

World.title: New 'landmark' drug shown to prevent recurrence of deadly melanoma
World.content:
Two US pharmaceutical giants, Merck and Moderna, say an experimental melanoma drug that delivers treatment tailored to a patient's specific tumour prevented the deadly form of skin cancer from returning in a large clinical trial.

Called "intismeran autogene," it is based on the same messenger ribonucleic acid technology behind Covid-19 vaccines.

Researchers have been working on developing mRNA treatments against cancer, but this is the first time one has shown positive results in a Phase 3 trial.

When delivered along with pembrolizumab, an immunotherapy drug and the current standard of care, intismeran autogene prevented melanoma recurrence and prevented the cancer from spreading to other organs, the companies said in a statement.

The news sent shares in Moderna soaring 128 per cent to $US143 ($200) while Merck's stock was up more than 10 per cent to $US149.50.

The new drug is based off of a similar technology that Moderna and other pharmaceutical companies used for their Covid-19 vaccines. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

The trial lasted approximately a year and involved 1,137 patients who, following surgical removal of their cancers, were randomised into groups, with two-thirds receiving the new treatment plus pembrolizumab, while the rest received pembrolizumab alone.

The companies said they would present their data at an upcoming international conference and begin filings with regulators for approval.

Professor Georgina Long, the study's principal investigator and medical director of Melanoma Institute Australia said in a statement that the "results represent a landmark moment for adjuvant melanoma treatment".

How often should you be reapplying sunscreen? What three experts had to say about how to get the best protection from your sunscreen this summer.

"Intismeran in combination with pembrolizumab has the potential to establish a new treatment paradigm in the adjuvant melanoma setting, helping patients remain cancer-free for longer," she added.

The treatment works by taking a sample of the patient's tumour and identifying its unique mutational signature, or "fingerprint," then using messenger RNA technology to fight it.

Messenger RNA technology uses synthetic molecular instructions wrapped in tiny fat bubbles to teach the body how to make specific proteins.

The technology came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Moderna and Pfizer developed vaccines that were highly effective against serious forms of the illness.

Melanoma is one of the deadliest forms of skin cancer, with more than 330,000 new cases diagnosed worldwide in 2022.

"Together with Merck, we are now studying intismeran in combination with pembrolizumab and other anti-cancer therapies, and as a monotherapy, across multiple tumour types and stages of disease, including melanoma, lung, bladder and kidney cancers," Moderna chief executive Stephane Bancel said in a statement.

AFP

World.title: Roblox to face external audits to prove it's safe for Australian children
World.content:
Australia's internet regulator has secured a court-enforceable undertaking from Roblox to improve protections against grooming and sexual exploitation, after tests found adult strangers could still contact children despite safety measures introduced by the world's biggest gaming platform.

The agreement marks an incremental win for the eSafety Commissioner it seeks to use its enforcement powers to make online platforms comply with Australia's sweeping child-safety rules, including a landmark ban on social media for children under 16.

In a statement released on Thursday, the eSafety Commissioner said its testing found adults could send connection requests to young Australian children on Roblox without parental consent, while children and adults could interact on forums outside games without parental approval.

What apps are banned in Australia? Ten platforms are included in Australia's world-first social media ban for under 16s.

Children's connections, profiles and other information were also visible to other users.

The regulator gave Roblox three months to roll out measures including stopping adults from contacting unknown children without parental consent, making children's accounts private by default and improving systems for reporting complaints and notifying users of outcomes.

The San Mateo, California-headquartered company must also hire an independent third-party auditor to assess the effectiveness of its safety measures, including its age-estimation technology.

eSafety said this was the first time it required an external safety audit by a tech firm.

"Roblox cannot mark their own homework," eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant said in a statement.

If Roblox breaches the undertaking, eSafety can apply to the Federal Court for an order requiring the company to comply, as well as seek other orders, the regulator added.

A Roblox spokesperson said the platform had "delivered on the commitments we made to eSafety over the last 12 months and (we) will continue to work towards our shared goal of keeping Australian children safe online".

It is not the first time Roblox has ended up in the sights of Australia's internet regulator, with eSafety releasing a statement earlier this year saying it had put the gaming platform "on notice" over child safety.

Last September, Roblox told eSafety it was putting in place nine specific commitments designed to keep children on its services safee.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Sacked Ukraine defence minister calls for wartime presidential election
World.content:
Ukraine's ousted Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for a wartime election, arguing Ukraine faces a "crisis of governance".

It is the first demand of its kind and would be the first leadership challenge to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Under Ukrainian law, holding elections during wartime is prohibited.

But in Mr Fedorov's video address he said "democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia".

"We must find a legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to renew its full democratic process even in the conditions of a long war," he said.

Zelenskyy just scored an 'own goal' The Ukrainian president's decision to fire his popular, tech-savvy 35-year-old Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week baffled many. Analysts say what happens next could be pivotal to the war.

The 35-year-old was a longtime ally of Mr Zelenskyy's until his unexpected firing from the Defence Ministry in July, just six months after he was appointed.

He was the last remaining member of Mr Zelenskyy's first cabinet in 2019.

Unlike his predecessors, Mr Fedorov publicly laid out a strategy to defeat Russia through attrition and technological superiority.

Shortly after his dismissal, a bitter rift was exposed between Mr Fedorov and the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

Protests have been held in Kyiv against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's decision to replace Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister. (Reuters: Thomas Peter)

Mixed reaction to idea of a wartime election

Thousands of Ukrainians then took to the streets demanding the sacking of Mr Syrskyi, who Mr Zelenskyy later dismissed bowing to public pressure.

Protests in support of Mr Fedorov have continued for the past month in Ukraine.

While Mr Fedorov did not say whether he would stand in an election, one recent poll has indicated the ex-minister could comfortably beat Mr Zelenskyy in a runoff vote, where the top two presidential candidates went head-to-head.

Protesters demand the reinstatement of Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister last month. (Reuters: Thomas Peter)

Mr Fedorov said Ukraine faced a "systemic crisis of governance".

"The old system lives by its own rules too often. It protects itself. It is scared of change," he said in his video address.

There has been mixed reaction to the idea of a wartime election within Ukraine.

A poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology earlier this month showed 57 per cent of Ukrainians believed elections should only take place after the war, given that hundreds of thousands of troops were on the front line.

Lesia Bidochko, a policy fellow at the European Policy Institute in Kyiv, said there was still no realistic way to organise a vote, with millions of Ukrainians also living as refugees overseas, displaced within the country, and serving in the military.

"Currently, it looks like an elegant way of occupying the opposition space without taking responsibility for the mechanics," she said.

Mr Zelenskyy's office had no immediate comment on Mr Fedorov's address.

New Ukraine defence minister appointed

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, newly appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi, his predecessor General Oleksandr Syrskyi, and new Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara at a meeting last month. (Supplied: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service)

Mr Fedorov's statement came just hours after new Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara, a former top special forces operative, was appointed.

He was not Mr Zelenskyy's primary pick for defence minister and was named as a placeholder only after the protests broke out.

Best known as the mastermind of Ukraine's deep strikes into Russia, Mr Khmara steps into the role as Kyiv struggles to defend against mounting Russian ballistic-missile attacks and grinding advances on the front line.

Mr Khmara's appointment also took place just hours after anti-corruption authorities announced charges against a deputy chief of Mr Zelenskyy's office as part of an alleged $4.2 million money-laundering scheme.

Ukraine's anti-corruption authorities revealed they had uncovered a group, including a deputy head of the presidential office, as part of their investigation into an alleged kickback scheme at the state atomic energy agency.

The anti-graft agencies did not name the official, but Mr Zelenskyy dismissed adviser Iryna Mudra shortly after the probe was announced last November.

She has not yet publicly commented on the matter.

Reuters

World.title: Israeli military clears soldiers over Gaza strike that killed Zomi Frankcom
World.content:
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has cleared its personnel of any criminal wrongdoing in the April 2024 strike on a World Central Kitchen (WCK) convoy in Gaza, where Australian woman Zomi Frankcom was killed.

The IDF said it had concluded there were serious failures that led soldiers to falsely identify a Hamas fighter was travelling in the convoy, which prompted an attack that killed seven humanitarian workers.

The armed man travelling with the vehicles was a security guard "to protect it from seizure by armed actors in Gaza," the IDF said in its statement.

But it said the presence of that guard had not been flagged with the IDF prior to the convoy setting off, and the vehicles later took a different route to what had been coordinated prior with the military.

"Accordingly, and in light of the assessment that Hamas operatives had taken control of the convoy before its arrival at the warehouse, the IDF mistakenly believed that the vehicles contained Hamas military operatives and therefore struck the vehicles," it said.

The military argued it had tried to contact WCK about the incident, but did not hear back.

"Notwithstanding serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."

Two commanders had already been stripped of their ranks as colonel and major, and a colonel, a major general and a brigadier general had also been reprimanded.

The ABC has contacted the Australian government for comment.

Just before the IDF announcement, Foreign Minister Penny Wong was marking World Humanitarian Day at an event in Parliament House in Canberra, where she launched an award in Ms Frankcom's honour in the presence of her family.

"I want to say to you that we will stand with you, and we will stand with you in years to come," Ms Wong said.

"I want to make it clear that the Australian government continues to press the Israeli Government for full accountability for the deaths of Zomi and her World Central Kitchen colleagues."

Zomi Frankcom volunteered with World Central Kitchen during the Black Summer bushfires. (Supplied: Kelly Eastwood)

Founder José Andrés said in the days following the attack "this was not just a bad luck situation where 'oops' we dropped the bomb in the wrong place".

"This was over 1.5, 1.8 kilometres, with a very defined humanitarian convoy that had signs in the top, in the roof, a very colourful logo that we are obviously very proud of," Mr Andrés said

"[It's] very clear who we are and what we do."

He described the IDF targeting each car, one-by-one, corralling the aid workers to the third car before it was ultimately struck.

Also killed in the strike were Palestinian Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha, Damian Sobol from Poland, US-Canadian national Jacob Flickinger and John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby from the UK.

A 2024 Australian government review into the incident found the IDF strike was a result of "serious failures to follow procedures".

It found there was a "significant break down in situational awareness", however ultimately ruled the strike was "not knowingly or deliberately directed" against the WCK.

Seven people were killed in the strike. (AP: Abdel Kareem Hana)

On March 31, the family of Lalzawmi "Zomi" Frankcom commemorated two years since her killing.

"There hasn't been any kind of justice served or any movement with the case," her brother Mal Frankcom told Radio National Breakfast at the time

" It's going to be painful every year, but having that would provide some kind of comfort. "

WCK condemned the IDF findings and said it fundamentally disagreed with the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation.

"There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so, it said in a statement.

"The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive.”

The organisation insisted the IDF knew its team was unarmed and did not pose a threat, yet still launched multiple airstrikes.

"The military investigation conflates different timelines and events, muddies the story and shifts the blame for the IDF’s illegal conduct,” WCK said, accusing the IDF of being incapable of investigating its own conduct.

Hind Rajab case prompts criminal probe

The IDF released details of five major investigations all at once on Wednesday afternoon, Israel time, and acknowledged for the first time it had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab.

The military said it would launch a criminal investigation into the January 2024 killing — a case which sparked worldwide outrage.

Hind was trapped in the wreckage of her family's car for hours, along with the bodies of six family members, and had desperately called for help.

Paramedics who travelled to the scene were also attacked, killing two paramedics.

US holds talks in bid to salvage Gaza peace plan Jared Kushner and Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed putting a US general in charge of verifying Hamas's disarmaments, with Israel's military to remain place until that happens.

The bodies were recovered almost two weeks later.

The finding of the IDF investigation suggested the criminal probe would be limited in its scope.

"Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division."

Buried paramedics investigation also released

The IDF also said it had recommended a criminal investigation into an attack by the military on a convoy of Palestinian paramedics in Tel al-Sultan in March 2025, in which 15 people were killed.

The wreckage of the ambulances the group was travelling in, along with the remains of those killed, was buried by soldiers in a shallow mass grave.

At the time of the attack, the IDF claimed that the vehicles had been travelling without their emergency lights flashing.

Video recovered from a phone of one of the killed paramedics proved otherwise, recording the moments the convoy arrived at the scene and the lengthy assault by Israeli forces which followed.

Israeli authorities continue to insist six Hamas fighters were among those killed in the attack.

"The firing conducted during the incident raises a reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct," the IDF said.

The Palestinian Red Crescent Society repeated its calls "for the formation of an independent international commission of inquiry to uncover the circumstances of this crime.”

It said there needed to be "full protection for medical teams” wherever they work around the world.

Two investigations into the killing of Médecins Sans Frontières staff in Khan Younis in February 2024 and Gaza City November 2023 also cleared personnel of criminal wrongdoing.

World.title: Opera for the Dead and ocean-inspired works shine at Art Music Awards
World.content:
Melbourne-based experimental group Chamber Made has come out on top as the biggest winner of the 2026 Art Music Awards, held on 19 August in Melbourne.

The arts organisation picked up two awards: Excellence in Experimental Practice for its 2025 presentations and artist development activities, and the Victorian State Luminary Award for its incredible 35-year history of shaping Australian music and performance.

The ocean was a recurring theme for three of the evening’s winners.

Paul Stanhope's epic Mahāsāgar (the Hindi word for ocean) received the award for Work of the Year: Choral.

Alex Turley's the ocean's dream of itself for mezzo-soprano and orchestra won Work of the Year: Large Ensemble, while Dark Oceanography, created by Kate Milligan and a team of artists and climate science researchers was awarded Work of the Year: Electroacoustic/Sound Art.

Familiar names dominate Work of the Year awards

Other Work of the Year honours went to names familiar to ABC Classic audiences, including Anne Cawrse, whose Killing the Angel in the House, composed for 2022 ABC Young Performers Awards winner Eliza Shephard, won Work of the Year: Solo & Small Ensemble.

Other recipients included Nat Bartsch, Mindy Meng Wang and Monica Lim, as well as first-time winner Noemi Liba Friedman.

First Nations-led collaboration takes out Performance of the Year

Leading the Performance of the Year winners was nyilamum song cycles, a First Nations-led collaboration by Dr Lou Bennett AM and Paul Stanhope.

Performed by the Australian String Quartet and Yorta Yorta, Dja Dja Wurrung artist and academic Dr Bennett, it received the award for Performance of the Year: Classical & Experimental.

Nick Russoniello was awarded Performance of the Year: Soloist for his performance of his own composition, Air Mass Suite.

In Performance of the Year: Jazz & Improvised Music, The Cloud Maker took top honours for its performance of the work of the same name.

Leadership in Art Music celebrated with several awards

Internationally acclaimed Australian composer, educator and researcher, Professor Liza Lim AM, received the prestigious Richard Gill Award for Distinguished Services to Australian Music in recognition of her visionary contribution to Australian art music.

There were also several Luminary Awards, which recognised artists and organisations whose vision, leadership and commitment continue to shape Australian music across the country.

Musica Viva Australia was awarded the National Luminary Award (Organisation), and Daryl Buckley received the National Luminary Award (Individual).

The ceremony, organised by APRA AMCOS and the Australian Music Centre, was held on August 19 at The Timber Yard in Melbourne.

This year's awards were hosted by Namila Benson, with guest presenters Aura Go and Connor D'Netto, and music curation by Sia Ahmad.

World.title: Graffiti 'wrongly' labelled antisemitic in Sydney spree, judge finds
World.content:
A man who admitted to a string of vandalism offences in Sydney's east did not act as an "antisemitic bigot" but was a "vandal for hire", and is not at risk of committing a serious terrorism offence, according to the state's highest court.

The NSW Supreme Court has dismissed an application by the State to place Mohommed Farhat under a year-long extended supervision order at the expiration of his jail sentence.

Had the application succeeded, it would have seen 55 strict conditions imposed on the 22-year-old, which would have been "highly restrictive" of his liberty.

Farhat pleaded guilty to 15 offences over the vandalism at Woollahra in November 2024, when vehicles were sprayed with slogans including "F*** Israel" and "PKK coming".

He was previously handed a sentence of one year and eight months with an expiry date in October 2026, and the State Parole Authority revoked his statutory parole due to a finding he posed a serious, identifiable risk to the safety of the community.

But Farhat has long claimed he was manipulated into the crimes and motivated by promises of money and drugs.

A Local Court judge previously said material before that court cast some doubt on the true motivation, but made a finding that a hatred of or prejudice against Jewish people was an aggravating factor.

The words "f*** Israel" were defaced on vehicles and property damaged, the judge said. (ABC News: Alison Xiao)

This week, Justice Desmond Fagan found that Farhat was "incited and directed" by another person to commit his crimes for a $4,000 payment and unspecified quantity of drugs.

He "did not intend to express hatred of Jews", the judge said in his reasons.

The judge also went on to find that the "f*** Israel" slogans were "objectively, crude expressions of political hostility to the state of Israel" and constituted a "curse against a foreign state".

"They are not antisemitic according to the ordinary understanding of that concept in the Australian community," Justice Fagan said.

"The fact that in this case the slogans were graffitied in a locality where a high proportion of residents may be Jewish does not imbue the curse with an antisemitic character."

Antisemitism definition criticised

Also in his reasons, Justice Fagan noted expert opinion before the court stated the definition of exactly what constitutes antisemitism was debated.

An analyst of middle eastern affairs, whose report was tendered by the Crown, made reference to a definition adopted by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA).

But Justice Fagan said the IHRA's formulation did not assist him in Farhat's case and "does not reflect the established usage and understanding of the term 'antisemitic' in Australia".

"The IHRA core text is so verbose and imprecise that it could not realistically be attributed to the ordinary, reasonably informed member of the Australian public," he said.

The judge said he was not the first to criticise the "inept drafting" of the IHRA formulation, noting that in a submission to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, the Jewish Council of Australia (JCA) also criticised the wording and cited detailed critiques by others.

"Discussion of the IHRA wording and adoption of it by some institutions does not change the established meaning of a word that has been in use in the English language for 150 years," Justice Fagan said.

"The IHRA formulation propounds a concept different from that which 'antisemitism' has long been understood to describe and appropriates that word to the novel concept."

The court concluded that Australians who strongly disapprove of Israel's treatment of Palestinians "have freedom to express their views", and others who support Israel have the right not to listen, read or engage.

In Farhat's case, the judge found, the words "f*** Israel" were conveyed by defacing vehicles and damaging property, which meant the seriousness of the crime was "increased by its wantonness, vulgarity and intimidatory effect but not by any antisemitic implication".

'Label has been wrongly applied'

Justice Fagan said police statements and intelligence reports had "uniformly" described Farhat's spray-painting as antisemitic, and that was then taken up by the prosecution's submissions to the Local Court "without reflection or analysis".

Justice Fagan expressed the view, respectfully, that the Local Court judge made a legal error in finding that "f*** Israel" was an antisemitic phrase and reflective of hatred of prejudice towards Jewish people.

The characterisation of the graffiti as being antisemitic led to Farhat being treated differently under criminal law, Justice Fagan said.

"The label has been wrongly applied, injustice to the defendant has followed and the misconception has led to the State bringing these proceedings," he said.

In a letter to the Local Court, Farhat previously wrote that at the time of the vandalism, he was "lost in my ways", addicted to drugs, and did not realise the gravity of his actions or the effect on others, particularly the Jewish and Turkish communities.

He said visits from a Jewish community member had "really opened my eyes" and allowed him to look at things from the perspectives of others.

"At the time of my offending I did not understand the deep meaning of my actions and their impact," he wrote.

"My whole life was taken over by drugs and negative influences."

World.title: Kyrgios provisionally suspended after positive cocaine test in Spain
World.content:
Australian tennis star Nick Kyrgios has said he tested positive for cocaine on the Spanish island of Mallorca and has issued an apology.

In a statement on his Instagram, he announced he "made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it".

"I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me," Kyrgios said.

"Above all I'm sorry to the kids who follow me.

" I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed with myself. "

The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) issued a statement revealing Kyrgios had been "provisionally suspended" since August 4.

"31-year-old Kyrgios provided a sample during an ATP 250 event in Mallorca, Spain, on 22 June 2026," it said.

"On 17 July 2026, a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory confirmed the presence of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine."

"Kyrgios, who reached a career-high world singles ranking of 13 in October 2016, has the right to appeal the provisional suspension, but has not done so to date," the ITIA said.

"As with all Tennis Anti-Doping Programme cases, ITIA support is available to Kyrgios.

"While suspended, Kyrgios is not allowed to play in, coach at, or attend any events organised or sanctioned by World Tennis, WTA, ATP, the Grand Slams, or any national association."

Nick Kyrgios has been open with his struggles with mental health in the past, including with depression and suicidal ideation. (Reuters: Amr Alfiky)

Kyrgios explained the incident came in the context of years "of injuries … both physically and mentally".

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined."

Kyrgios has spoken publicly about his previous struggles with mental health, telling the BBC in 2022 he struggled with alcohol and drug abuse, as well as depression and self-harm.

He has won seven ATP singles titles and the 2022 Australian Open doubles title, partnering with Thanasi Kokkinakis.

In July 2026, he lost in the first round of men's doubles at Wimbledon and later said it was probably his last appearance at the competition.

"I would probably say pretty confidently my last Wimbledon," Kyrgios said.

"It would be hard to see myself coming back here again and competing.

"That [2022] final was always going to be one of the better memories of my tennis career, but I just can't see myself getting back to anywhere near that level.

"I've always said I didn't choose tennis, tennis chose me," Kyrgios said.

"But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I've ever had to face.

" At times I've felt helpless and alone. None of that excuses what I did. "

He said the "good news" was his drug test failure and suspension "has given me a wake-up call" and said he would step away from social media and the public spotlight for the next 28 days.

"I'd ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly the privacy of my family," he said.

"I'm sorry.

"I'll do the work and come back better."

World.title: Oil prices spike after ships in Strait of Hormuz hit by fresh strikes
World.content:
Three ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz have been attacked in recent days, British maritime officials said.

The ships were struck by unknown projectiles, resulting in two casualties, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.

INTERCARGO, an association of cargo shipowners, reported that a sailor aboard the Liberian-flagged bulk carrier Minoan Dynasty was killed on Monday.

The Strait of Hormuz saw roughly a fifth of the world's oil pass through it before the war. (ABC News Graphics)

While hostilities between Iran and the United States have eased in recent weeks, a string of attacks on vessels passing through the strait has unsettled investors, pushing oil prices to a three-week high.

Brent crude futures jumped more than 3 per cent over the past week, to $US91.38 by 5:45pm AEST on Friday.

The narrow waterway between Iran and Oman is a vital shipping route for oil in the region.

Amid fresh strikes on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz and stalled peace talks, oil prices have spiked. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Uncertainty over passage through strait

Iran's top negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, said on state media yesterday the strait will remain shut until the US meets the conditions of an interim deal signed between the two countries in June.

The conditions include the US lifting its own blockade, removing oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and ending military threats, he told parliament.

However, last week, Saudi Aramco, the world's top oil producer, resumed loading oil from inside the strait, eyeing Singapore and Malaysia as potential destinations.

Saudi Aramco resumed shipping through the strait last week. (AP: Hassan Ammar)

Despite Iran and the US not directly trading blows, energy prices have remained higher than pre-war levels while the roughly 500 million barrels that usually flow through the strait each month slowed to a trickle.

In a rally speech on Friday, US President Donald Trump said Americans should prepare for higher petrol prices as the war continues.

Shipping through the contested strait has slowed further in recent days, following similar attacks on vessels last week and talks between Iran and the US stalling.

Mr Trump said there are no talks planned between the two countries, and insisted the strait was open.

Donald Trump has repeatedly said throughout the war that the strait is open, saying the US controls the shipping routes. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

"The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated," he said on Truth Social yesterday.

" There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled with the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Naval Blockage remains in full force and effect. "

A ceasefire between Iran and the US expired on Monday, and Mr Trump said he would not be extending it.

The president also said that the US would claim the strait as a US territory after the war.

Trump says Strait of Hormuz to become US territory US President Donald Trump says he will soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, escalating his rhetoric over the vital waterway that carries a significant share of global oil supplies.

Trump upping the rhetoric

The strait is becoming a point of stress for the American president, as the ongoing Iran war becomes increasingly unpopular at home.

He recently threatened to bomb US ally Oman, saying: "If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the shit out of them", in an interview with Fox News.

Oman, whose coastline is a part of the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran have been discussing opening the strait for weeks.

Six months into the conflict, 17 seafarers have died in the waterway according to the UN, with the number of ships passing through estimated to have dropped by roughly 90 per cent.

Many ships travel with their navigation and identification devices turned off to make them harder to attack.

"Seafarers are civilians and must never become targets or collateral victims of geopolitical conflicts," INTERCARGO said in a statement.

" One seafarer lost is one too many. "

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Judge finds King Eddies negligent after catastrophic birth-injury but rules against compensation payout
World.content:
NationalWACourts Judge finds King Eddies negligent after catastrophic birth-injury but rules against compensation payout Rebecca Peppiatt August 20, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Perth family has lost a catastrophic birth-injury lawsuit against a major maternity hospital despite a judge finding clinicians were negligent, after a court ruled their daughter’s severe brain damage was legally “inevitable.” The girl, whom WAtoday has chosen not to name, was born in August 2020 at 38-weeks gestation due to issues picked up during a routine examination at King Edward Memorial Hospital in Subiaco. King Edward Memorial Hospital. An ultrasound had shown growth restriction, reduced amniotic fluid and abnormal cerebral blood flow that pointed to the unborn baby being in distress and doctors advised the parents she should be delivered early. How the baby would be born was then discussed with hospital staff, and a dispute over whether the parents were offered an induced natural labour or an elective caesarean began.



The parents later told the Supreme Court of WA that they were told an elective caesarean was “not an option in a public hospital”. However, the court preferred the evidence of the doctors, finding that an elective caesarean was available but the parents declined it by choice. Court documents showed the mother held a strong preference for a vaginal birth so was later induced, but monitoring of the baby’s heart rate showed she was in distress and needed to be delivered urgently with an emergency caesarean. Doctors stated that the father spent the next 20 to 30 minutes asking questions about the risks of the surgery. The baby’s distressed state continued, with medical notes showing her heart rate was deteriorating and her delivery became a category-1 emergency.



Despite the extreme urgency, the father continued questioning the doctors for another five to 10 minutes, the documents claimed. The mother then gave oral consent, but only after a physical examination confirmed her cervix was not sufficiently dilated and a vaginal birth was no longer possible. As she was being wheeled into the operating theatre after signing the consent form, doctors told the court that the father kept the form, edited it and crossed out two deletions of standard clauses that included consent for clinical photographs and vaginal examinations by supervised medical students under anaesthesia. Surgical staff were then under pressure to find the consent form without knowing the father still had it, with allegations that the surgeon declared he had to go ahead without the form because it was an emergency. Doctors told the court that this delayed carrying out the caesarean, but the father disputed the evidence and said he handed it over the first time it was asked.



The delay in obtaining consent proved fatal to the family’s legal case. Related Article Courts WA couple win Supreme Court battle to become same-sex parents through surrogacy The family argued that the hospital was negligent in failing to recognise the earlier need for a caesarean. However, the judge ruled that because a doctor cannot legally perform surgery without consent, and because the parents’ pattern of questioning took approximately 30 minutes to resolve, recommending a caesarean earlier would not have resulted in an earlier delivery. The court concluded that the mother would not have consented any earlier than she did, meaning the baby’s injuries were legally “inevitable” and not caused by the hospital’s prior negligence.



Despite this, the judge still ruled that the hospital was legally negligent because it breached its duty of care when a midwife paged the registrar to review a highly concerning heart trace. The court found that the doctor did not review the CTG history, did not speak to the midwife, and did not ask why she had been paged. Instead, she did no more than “glance” at the screen and left the room. The judge ruled that this complete failure to undertake an interpretation of the CTG fell short of the precautions a reasonable hospital would have taken to mitigate the risk of oxygen deprivation. However, the claim was dismissed because the judge ultimately found the baby’s hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury was unavoidable and not caused by the hospital’s actions.



The little girl, now five years- old, survived a prolonged resuscitation but was left with grade-three brain damage, cerebral palsy, functional blindness, and impaired hearing. Her parents pursued legal action in order to secure financial compensation to help support their daughter, who has ongoing impairments likely to persist for the rest of her life. The judge closed his remarks by acknowledging his findings would be “of little consolation” to a family left wondering how their daughter suffered profound injuries while in the hospital’s care. A GoFundMe page has raised almost $7000 of a $55,000 target for the girl to have “breakthrough treatment” overseas to stimulate her brain and potentially offer improvements in her quality of life. Her father wrote that she “continues to show strength, awareness and joy”, adding that “her resilience is beyond words”.

World.title: No criminal probe over Israeli strike that killed Australian Zomi Frankcom
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIsraeli-Palestinian conflict No criminal probe over Israeli strike that killed Australian Zomi Frankcom Sarah McPhee August 20, 2026 — 12:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Israel’s military has cleared its personnel of any criminal wrongdoing over an April 2024 strike in Gaza which killed seven aid workers including Australian Zomi Frankcom. The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) released a series of decisions on Wednesday regarding five incidents including the deaths of the World Central Kitchen (WCK) workers, and whether it would conduct criminal investigations. Australian Zomi Frankcom was killed in a 2024 airstrike while delivering aid in Gaza with World Central Kitchen. Frankcom, 43, and six colleagues died on April 1, 2024 when the vehicle they were travelling in was fired upon while delivering aid in Gaza. The IDF said its officers had “mistakenly believed that the vehicles contained Hamas military operatives and therefore struck the vehicles”.



It claimed that attempts were made to contact WCK representatives during “the approximately half-hour period in which the convoy vehicles were tracked on the understanding that they contained Hamas operatives”, but those attempts were unsuccessful. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘We have expressed sympathy’: Israeli ambassador declines to apologise for Zomi Frankcom killing The Israeli military said the presence of armed security to accompany the convoy “was not coordinated with IDF authorities” and the vehicles had deviated from the route arranged in advance, while several people were also mistakenly identified as armed persons. “Following review of all findings of the factual assessment, it was determined that, notwithstanding serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct,” the IDF said. It added that there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation”.



Two Israeli officers were dismissed from their positions and three senior officers were formally reprimanded, according to the Israeli military. World Central Kitchen said it fundamentally disagreed with the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation. “We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024,” the aid organisation said in a statement. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive.” Earlier on Wednesday, and prior to the IDF’s statement, Foreign Minister Penny Wong spoke at a Parliament House event attended by Frankcom’s family as she launched the Zomi Frankcom Humanitarian Award.



Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu bluntly rejects Trump’s Gaza plan to disarm Hamas “I want to make it clear that the Australian government continues to press the Israeli government for full accountability for the deaths of Zomi and her World Central Kitchen colleagues,” Wong said. “Zomi and her family deserve justice.” In a report released in July 2024, former Australian Defence Force chief Mark Binskin found that “a significant breakdown in situational awareness” by the Israeli military caused the strike that killed Frankcom, adding he did not believe the charity workers were deliberately targeted. The IDF said its Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism had reviewed approximately 150 incidents since the beginning of the war, then transferred them for examination by the Military Prosecution. It said it would conduct criminal investigations into the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab and her family, who were trapped in a vehicle in Gaza City and pleaded for help by phone in January 2024, and the killing of 15 Palestinian paramedics as they drove in the southern city of Rafah in March 2025.



The military also decided not to take criminal action over the killings of four staffers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate instances in November 2023 and February 2024. with Reuters/AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
