World.title: Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m of CBA shares amid separation from wife
World.content:
NationalCBD Opinion Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m of CBA shares amid separation from wife John Buckley CBD columnist August 19, 2026 — 9:20pm

August 19, 2026 — 9:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Executives sell shares in their own companies all the time. So when Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn offloaded about $8.4 million worth of shares last week, we didn’t think much of it. But that was before we knew Comyn and his wife, Lucy, are working through the terms of their separation, which CBD brought word of on Tuesday, after the Commonwealth Bank confirmed the couple had split. Commonwealth Bank chief Matt Comyn presents the bank’s full year 2026 results. Nic Long The share disclosure, released to the market on August 14, showed Comyn acquired a tick over 30,000 shares as a result of vested equity earned as part of his remuneration. Then there were two tranches of shares sold: The first tranche of 30,006 shares sold at $168.18 per share, worth a little over $5 million. The second lot of 20,091 shares went at $168.80, worth about $3.4 million. All up, the share movement leaves Comyn’s direct shareholding about the same as it was the day before, and is not out of step with his previous share sales, which have occurred at least once a year since 2022. A Commonwealth Bank spokesman declined to comment on whether Comyn’s share sale this month was related to his separation.



But our guess is the sale, the second tranche of which was jointly held by Comyn and his wife as beneficiaries of a trust, freed up a helpful chunk of cash for whatever costs are racked up through the separation, and, of course, may make it easier for the couple to split their assets. Another Pauline whisperer It was only June when we last brought word of the frenzy among corporates to find so-called “Pauline whisperers” to cosy up to One Nation as the party rises in the polls. Well, it looks like business is good enough for those who already have a line into One Nation leader Pauline Hanson to flaunt their access. One lobbyist who has since made the pitch for those betting that Hanson’s popularity will hold out until at least 2028 is Jannette Cotterell, who set up her lobby shop Executive Counsel Australia back in 2008 following a five-year stint at CT Group, formerly known as Crosby Textor.



Cotterell describes herself as non-partisan, and in a post to LinkedIn felt it necessary to declare “engagement does not equal endorsement”. We bet! When reached on Tuesday, Cotterell was quick to have a crack at us over the sausagefest of names that populated our last column item on the matter. She was also quick to take the opportunity to pump up her own tyres. But we’ll spare you the marketing material. Cotterral’s name joins a string of others who have been bandied about in political circles as possible One Nation relationship brokers. So far we’ve heard the name of Gina Rinehart’s media minder James Radford come up. So too former Nationals deputy campaign director and conservative lobbyist Michael Kauter. Also: Scott Mitchell, who spent five years as the federal director of the Nationals before setting up his own lobby shop. We’re sure they’re freshening up their pitch decks. Life after Ley Former opposition leader Sussan Ley’s ex-spinner Liam Jones may be having a little trouble letting go of his old life, as CBD brought word of last week.



But it looks like Ley’s former chief of staff Dean Shachar has had no such trouble moving on – to a meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, no less. On Wednesday, Shachar was quick to brag about his rendezvous with Albanese in Canberra in a post to LinkedIn, after the PM was able to squeeze in some time in the diary to hear all about Shachar’s new employer, the retail share trading platform, Superhero. But apparently it wasn’t just Albo and Shachar there to chew the fat. Also present were the company’s co-founders, chief executive John Winters and chief technology officer Wayne Baskin, who presented Albo with a Hawthorn Football Club jersey. The Superhero founders were simply flogging their own wares, given the company is a back-of-jersey sponsor. But who knows, given Albo’s approach to politics, the Hawks may be in with a shot to win over a new supporter. The PM wasn’t the only one who had to sit through the pitch. Winters and Shachar were also seen at Aussies on Thursday morning in talks with Chris Taylor, the newly minted chief of staff to One Nation leader Pauline Hanson. The Superhero guys also made overtures to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor’s office on Wednesday, CBD hears, and met with several Coalition MPs through the week.



Airwallex Cafe It would seem no idea is too corny for the Airwallex marketing team. There was the financial start-up’s bizarre co-sponsorship of a function on a yacht called “Mischief”. Then the company’s sponsorship of Essendon Football Club. Now the company has set up a pop-up cafe. But our guess is any idea that distracts from the audit announced by the nation’s financial crimes agency AUSTRAC this year is probably considered a good one. “Yeah, I mean look, it’s just a great opportunity where we know people are in town candidly, and like the majority of people here are customers,” the company’s Australia and New Zealand boss James Teodorini said on Wednesday. “We’re lucky – I was just speaking to someone who’s been a customer for nine years and they were like, want to come down and say hi. “Um, it’s an opportunity while people are in town. Not to go and necessarily do this versus that, but just talk about who we are.” Nice one.



The cafe was set up around the corner from the ICC in Sydney, where Airwallex’s rival payments company, Stripe, was hosting an event of its own. As far as stunts go, this has to be among the lamest. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWEducation Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors Ben Cubby and Emily Kowal Updated August 19, 2026 — 9:09pm ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scots College has hit back against claims from parents that the prestigious private school had reacted poorly to the ongoing sexual assault scandal because the families of some of the boys who have been charged were financial donors to the school. The students – a 13-year-old boy and two 14-year-old boys – were charged with aggravated sexual assault after an alleged attack on a girl in a Bondi Junction laneway on July 22. Some parents told the Herald they were concerned the school was downplaying the seriousness of the incident because of financial donations previously made by families of two of the three boys, who cannot be legally identified. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s “active and continuing” handling of the crisis, and said he intended to remain in his role until his planned retirement at the end of next year amid calls for his resignation.



“The suggestion that the college is shielding any student because of a family donation is false,” Lambert, who has held the title of school principal for 19 years, said in a statement. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s handling of the crisis. “Donations have no bearing whatsoever on decisions concerning student welfare, attendance or discipline. “The same standards apply to every student, with each case considered on its facts and in accordance with law, not according to family circumstances or public pressure.” One concerned parent with a student at the private boys’ school said the anger [among parents] was palpable.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Scots College briefs boys as young as 10 on sexual assault allegations as council backs principal “The accusation is horrifying and, of course, we worry about the effect on our boy, anybody would. The students will be tarred with same brush. Honestly, I think they would have had their enrolment looked into already if they hadn’t donated,” the parent said. Another parent said the school had failed to substantially address her questions about culture in relation to the alleged assault on July 22 and previous incidents at the elite institution. “I’m appalled at how the school has responded,” said the parent with a boy in the same year group as the three boys charged with sex offences. “It’s how you react when these things happen that define you. And the way that the school is reacting right now is appalling personally as a parent, as a woman, as a human being. You don’t have to be a woman.



“It’s just not the culture I want my son in.” The question of financial donations is considered sensitive by many in the school community because Scots College is heavily dependent on cash gifts from parents, with more than 400 names listed on the school’s donations register. The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations. Alex Donnini Philanthropic giving generally yields the school about $4 million to $6 million a year, according to its financial disclosures. However, much larger sums have been obtained from the school community to fund capital works programs. The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations, including a gift of more than $12 million from Cunningham, a former student, management consultant and honorary consul general of Barbados in Australia.



Three other families gave more than $1 million each towards the building’s construction, while another 81 families, trusts and foundations kicked in tens of thousands each to get the project off the ground, according to school records. The median income of households with children at the Bellevue Hill school was $336,000 in 2024, and fees can be among the highest in the nation at more than $50,000 a year. Parents and former students said they could only speak anonymously of their concerns about the school’s culture because they were worried about a backlash against their children. Lambert said their fears were unfounded. “The college does not take disciplinary action against students because a parent or former student has lawfully expressed a concern or opinion about the college,” he said.



“We expect genuine concerns to be raised directly with the college so they can be answered, while every member of our community must protect young people’s privacy and welfare and respect the legal process.” It is not the first time Lambert has been forced to defend the school against claims of sexual assault by Scots College boys. In 2021, several Sydney private schools, including Scots, faced allegations raised in an online petition – launched by former Kambala student Chanel Contos – that students had assaulted young women. Related Article Opinion

Other students said they were physically forced to perform oral sex on a male while intoxicated, sometimes while the boy’s friends were present or filming the incident. World.title: Judge finds King Eddies negligent after catastrophic birth-injury but rules against compensation payout
World.content:
NationalWACourts Judge finds King Eddies negligent after catastrophic birth-injury but rules against compensation payout Rebecca Peppiatt August 20, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Perth family has lost a catastrophic birth-injury lawsuit against a major maternity hospital despite a judge finding clinicians were negligent, after a court ruled their daughter’s severe brain damage was legally “inevitable.” The girl, whom WAtoday has chosen not to name, was born in August 2020 at 38-weeks gestation due to issues picked up during a routine examination at King Edward Memorial Hospital in Subiaco. King Edward Memorial Hospital. An ultrasound had shown growth restriction, reduced amniotic fluid and abnormal cerebral blood flow that pointed to the unborn baby being in distress and doctors advised the parents she should be delivered early. How the baby would be born was then discussed with hospital staff, and a dispute over whether the parents were offered an induced natural labour or an elective caesarean began.



The parents later told the Supreme Court of WA that they were told an elective caesarean was “not an option in a public hospital”. However, the court preferred the evidence of the doctors, finding that an elective caesarean was available but the parents declined it by choice. Court documents showed the mother held a strong preference for a vaginal birth so was later induced, but monitoring of the baby’s heart rate showed she was in distress and needed to be delivered urgently with an emergency caesarean. Doctors stated that the father spent the next 20 to 30 minutes asking questions about the risks of the surgery. The baby’s distressed state continued, with medical notes showing her heart rate was deteriorating and her delivery became a category-1 emergency.



Despite the extreme urgency, the father continued questioning the doctors for another five to 10 minutes, the documents claimed. The mother then gave oral consent, but only after a physical examination confirmed her cervix was not sufficiently dilated and a vaginal birth was no longer possible. As she was being wheeled into the operating theatre after signing the consent form, doctors told the court that the father kept the form, edited it and crossed out two deletions of standard clauses that included consent for clinical photographs and vaginal examinations by supervised medical students under anaesthesia. Surgical staff were then under pressure to find the consent form without knowing the father still had it, with allegations that the surgeon declared he had to go ahead without the form because it was an emergency. Doctors told the court that this delayed carrying out the caesarean, but the father disputed the evidence and said he handed it over the first time it was asked.



The delay in obtaining consent proved fatal to the family’s legal case. Related Article Courts WA couple win Supreme Court battle to become same-sex parents through surrogacy The family argued that the hospital was negligent in failing to recognise the earlier need for a caesarean. However, the judge ruled that because a doctor cannot legally perform surgery without consent, and because the parents’ pattern of questioning took approximately 30 minutes to resolve, recommending a caesarean earlier would not have resulted in an earlier delivery. The court concluded that the mother would not have consented any earlier than she did, meaning the baby’s injuries were legally “inevitable” and not caused by the hospital’s prior negligence.



Despite this, the judge still ruled that the hospital was legally negligent because it breached its duty of care when a midwife paged the registrar to review a highly concerning heart trace. The court found that the doctor did not review the CTG history, did not speak to the midwife, and did not ask why she had been paged. Instead, she did no more than “glance” at the screen and left the room. The judge ruled that this complete failure to undertake an interpretation of the CTG fell short of the precautions a reasonable hospital would have taken to mitigate the risk of oxygen deprivation. However, the claim was dismissed because the judge ultimately found the baby’s hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury was unavoidable and not caused by the hospital’s actions.



The little girl, now five years- old, survived a prolonged resuscitation but was left with grade-three brain damage, cerebral palsy, functional blindness, and impaired hearing. Her parents pursued legal action in order to secure financial compensation to help support their daughter, who has ongoing impairments likely to persist for the rest of her life. The judge closed his remarks by acknowledging his findings would be “of little consolation” to a family left wondering how their daughter suffered profound injuries while in the hospital’s care. A GoFundMe page has raised almost $7000 of a $55,000 target for the girl to have “breakthrough treatment” overseas to stimulate her brain and potentially offer improvements in her quality of life. Her father wrote that she “continues to show strength, awareness and joy”, adding that “her resilience is beyond words”.

World.title: No criminal probe over Israeli strike that killed Australian Zomi Frankcom
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIsraeli-Palestinian conflict No criminal probe over Israeli strike that killed Australian Zomi Frankcom Sarah McPhee August 20, 2026 — 12:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Israel’s military has cleared its personnel of any criminal wrongdoing over an April 2024 strike in Gaza which killed seven aid workers including Australian Zomi Frankcom. The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) released a series of decisions on Wednesday regarding five incidents including the deaths of the World Central Kitchen (WCK) workers, and whether it would conduct criminal investigations. Australian Zomi Frankcom was killed in a 2024 airstrike while delivering aid in Gaza with World Central Kitchen. Frankcom, 43, and six colleagues died on April 1, 2024 when the vehicle they were travelling in was fired upon while delivering aid in Gaza. The IDF said its officers had “mistakenly believed that the vehicles contained Hamas military operatives and therefore struck the vehicles”.



It claimed that attempts were made to contact WCK representatives during “the approximately half-hour period in which the convoy vehicles were tracked on the understanding that they contained Hamas operatives”, but those attempts were unsuccessful. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘We have expressed sympathy’: Israeli ambassador declines to apologise for Zomi Frankcom killing The Israeli military said the presence of armed security to accompany the convoy “was not coordinated with IDF authorities” and the vehicles had deviated from the route arranged in advance, while several people were also mistakenly identified as armed persons. “Following review of all findings of the factual assessment, it was determined that, notwithstanding serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct,” the IDF said. It added that there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation”.



Two Israeli officers were dismissed from their positions and three senior officers were formally reprimanded, according to the Israeli military. World Central Kitchen said it fundamentally disagreed with the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation. “We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024,” the aid organisation said in a statement. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive.” Earlier on Wednesday, and prior to the IDF’s statement, Foreign Minister Penny Wong spoke at a Parliament House event attended by Frankcom’s family as she launched the Zomi Frankcom Humanitarian Award.



Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu bluntly rejects Trump’s Gaza plan to disarm Hamas “I want to make it clear that the Australian government continues to press the Israeli government for full accountability for the deaths of Zomi and her World Central Kitchen colleagues,” Wong said. “Zomi and her family deserve justice.” In a report released in July 2024, former Australian Defence Force chief Mark Binskin found that “a significant breakdown in situational awareness” by the Israeli military caused the strike that killed Frankcom, adding he did not believe the charity workers were deliberately targeted. The IDF said its Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism had reviewed approximately 150 incidents since the beginning of the war, then transferred them for examination by the Military Prosecution. It said it would conduct criminal investigations into the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab and her family, who were trapped in a vehicle in Gaza City and pleaded for help by phone in January 2024, and the killing of 15 Palestinian paramedics as they drove in the southern city of Rafah in March 2025.



The military also decided not to take criminal action over the killings of four staffers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate instances in November 2023 and February 2024. with Reuters/AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m worth of CBA shares amid separation from his wife
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m worth of CBA shares amid separation from his wife Fiona Byrne and John Buckley August 19, 2026 — 9:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Executives sell shares in their own companies all the time. So when Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn offloaded about $8.4 million worth of shares last week, we didn’t think much of it. But that was before we knew that Comyn and his wife, Lucy, were working through the terms of their separation, which CBD brought word of on Tuesday, after the Commonwealth Bank confirmed the couple had split. Commonwealth Bank CEO Matt Comyn has separated from his wife. Dominic Lorrimer The disclosure, which was released to the market on August 14, showed Comyn acquired a tick over 30,000 shares as a result of vested equity earned as part of his remuneration. Then there were two tranches of shares sold. The first tranche sold 30,006 shares at $168.18 per share, worth a little over $5 million. The second sold 20,091 shares at $168.80, worth about $3.4 million. All up, the share movement leaves Comyn’s direct shareholding about the same as it was the day before, and is not out of step with his previous share sales, which have occurred at least once a year since 2022. A Commonwealth Bank spokesman declined to comment on whether Comyn’s share sale this month was related to his separation.



But our guess is the sale, the second tranche of which was jointly held by Comyn and his wife as beneficiaries of a trust, freed up a helpful chunk of cash for whatever costs are racked up through the separation, and, of course, may make it easier for the couple to split their assets. No end in sight for Hughesy’s Liberal spruiking Politically activated comedian Dave Hughes is ramping up his Liberals spruiking tour and will join Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann for a Pub Talks event next month. While he continues to rule out ever standing for a seat and is not a Liberal Party member, Hughesy is in full campaign mode, and the more criticism he attracts for his anti-Labor rants and corruption-busting call-outs, the more he is leaning into his political epiphany. Dave Hughes has been making headlines for his criticism of Labor. Simon Schluter



He’s a preacher who has found his pulpit and is relentless. He’s had plenty of experience over the years doing press roll-outs for TV shows and his stand-up tours, so in some ways, pumping up Jess Wilson and the Libs’ tyres is just another type of publicity push for the former radio host. Related Article Victorian election Dave Hughes to campaign for Liberals in Victorian election “I think the Liberals are our best bet right now,” Hughesy told CBD last week when confirming he would back Wilson in November’s state election. Hughesy will be unleashed with Lindemann at a yet-to-be-revealed location on September 16. This is no laughing matter. “I’ve known him a long time, ” Lindemann said of his Hughesy connection when CBD called.



“I used to work in real estate in Altona and he was always looking for a property in the area. He never actually bought anything off me, but he was always enquiring. “I’ve been trying to nail him down for a while and finally he said, ‘All right, I’ll do it’.” Meanwhile, in an inevitable coming together of celebrities piping up about politics, Hughesy turned up where else but on Karl Stefanovic’s podcast on Wednesday night. Maggie T mementos up for grabs For decades, Maggie Tabberer was a beacon of elegance for Australian women – not to mention a two-time winner of the Gold Logie for her TV work – and now pieces of her legacy are up for grabs.



After her death in December 2024, Tabberer’s family are putting a curated collection of her jewellery under the hammer with Shapiro Auctioneers. It is the third auction of items from Tabberer’s sizeable estate. Fashion doyenne Maggie Tabberer. Of the 20 lots, CBD took note of the set of Cartier pens, one with the name Maggie T engraved on it, and a YSL wrist cuff with Maggie fashioned across it. It was custom-made for Tabberer by YSL. What’s the saying about what’s in a name? Other featured pieces include a strand of South Sea pearls, a long 18ct gold curb link necklace with nine charms which has an estimate of $20,000-25,000, and a set of Gucci pens. The distinctive necklace, with one of the charms being a large gold M, was one of Tabberer’s favourite jewellery pieces, CBD was informed. Other items for sale include rings, bracelets, watches and necklaces. As would be expected from Tabberer, it is a classy collection.



“She loved her life and she loved everything she owned,” Brooke Tabberer, Maggie’s daughter, told CBD. “They say every picture tells a story and there are many a story to each piece in the collection that is being offered. She was a lady of great style and good luck to the new owners.” A set of Cartier pens, one with the name ‘Maggie T’ engraved on the cap, owned by Maggie Tabberer is going to auction with Shapiro Auctioneers. Shapiro Auctioneers/supplied The pieces will be sold via online auction. Bidding is under way and will close on August 25. There was no sign, however, of Tabberer’s Gold Logies, which remain with her family.

World.title: Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWEducation Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors Ben Cubby and Emily Kowal Updated August 19, 2026 — 9:09pm ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scots College has hit back against claims from parents that the prestigious private school had reacted poorly to the ongoing sexual assault scandal because the families of some of the boys who have been charged were financial donors to the school. The students – a 13-year-old boy and two 14-year-old boys – were charged with aggravated sexual assault after an alleged attack on a girl in a Bondi Junction laneway on July 22. Some parents told the Herald they were concerned the school was downplaying the seriousness of the incident because of financial donations previously made by families of two of the three boys, who cannot be legally identified. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s “active and continuing” handling of the crisis, and said he intended to remain in his role until his planned retirement at the end of next year amid calls for his resignation.



“The suggestion that the college is shielding any student because of a family donation is false,” Lambert, who has held the title of school principal for 19 years, said in a statement. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s handling of the crisis. “Donations have no bearing whatsoever on decisions concerning student welfare, attendance or discipline. “The same standards apply to every student, with each case considered on its facts and in accordance with law, not according to family circumstances or public pressure.” One concerned parent with a student at the private boys’ school said the anger [among parents] was palpable.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Scots College briefs boys as young as 10 on sexual assault allegations as council backs principal “The accusation is horrifying and, of course, we worry about the effect on our boy, anybody would. The students will be tarred with same brush. Honestly, I think they would have had their enrolment looked into already if they hadn’t donated,” the parent said. Another parent said the school had failed to substantially address her questions about culture in relation to the alleged assault on July 22 and previous incidents at the elite institution. “I’m appalled at how the school has responded,” said the parent with a boy in the same year group as the three boys charged with sex offences. “It’s how you react when these things happen that define you. And the way that the school is reacting right now is appalling personally as a parent, as a woman, as a human being. You don’t have to be a woman.



“It’s just not the culture I want my son in.” The question of financial donations is considered sensitive by many in the school community because Scots College is heavily dependent on cash gifts from parents, with more than 400 names listed on the school’s donations register. The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations. Alex Donnini Philanthropic giving generally yields the school about $4 million to $6 million a year, according to its financial disclosures. However, much larger sums have been obtained from the school community to fund capital works programs. The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations, including a gift of more than $12 million from Cunningham, a former student, management consultant and honorary consul general of Barbados in Australia.



Three other families gave more than $1 million each towards the building’s construction, while another 81 families, trusts and foundations kicked in tens of thousands each to get the project off the ground, according to school records. The median income of households with children at the Bellevue Hill school was $336,000 in 2024, and fees can be among the highest in the nation at more than $50,000 a year. Parents and former students said they could only speak anonymously of their concerns about the school’s culture because they were worried about a backlash against their children. Lambert said their fears were unfounded. “The college does not take disciplinary action against students because a parent or former student has lawfully expressed a concern or opinion about the college,” he said.



“We expect genuine concerns to be raised directly with the college so they can be answered, while every member of our community must protect young people’s privacy and welfare and respect the legal process.” It is not the first time Lambert has been forced to defend the school against claims of sexual assault by Scots College boys. In 2021, several Sydney private schools, including Scots, faced allegations raised in an online petition – launched by former Kambala student Chanel Contos – that students had assaulted young women. World.title: How many portfolios can one minister handle?
World.content:
A law professor says 11 portfolios for one minister would be "completely unsustainable" during a political term, but its close enough to the election that it could work as a placeholder.

"It'll just be a case of keeping the car on the road rather than trying anything new."

University of Otago Law professor Andrew Geddis told RNZ it was "probably just the easiest and quickest thing to do" given the circumstances the prime minister was in last Wednesday.

He said in the normal course of governing - if it was at the start or the middle of a parliamentary term - it would "probably be completely unsustainable".

The fact there was less than three months until the election mean it was possible to do so as "placeholder" type role.

"But certainly, there is not going to be a huge amount of time for Paul Goldsmith to devote to each of his individual portfolios, let alone giving them all of the attention that they perhaps need."

University of Otago Law professor Andrew Geddis. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Goldsmith is now the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage, Minister of Defence, Minister Responsible for the GCSB, and for the NZSIS, Minister of Justice, Minister for Media and Communications, Minister for Pacific Peoples, Minister for Public Service and Digitising Government, Minister for Space, Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations and Minister for Veterans.

The Spinoff published on Wednesday a suggestion for Goldsmith's new schedule, including drinking three cups of coffee on Monday at 1.30am.

It also suggested he "think briefly about art" between 2.30am-2.33am and between 6pm-7pm he should "Google 'how to get Ngāpuhi to sign Treaty settlement'". On Tuesday between 5pm-11pm it suggested getting "yelled at by Winston Peters".

Asked if the schedule was accurate, Goldsmith said it was not.

"I'm pleased to see satire and comedy are still a feature of the political landscape," he added.

Geddis said Goldsmith would be receiving regular updates from his public servants, "so he'll get a heads up" as to the matters that are occurring within those portfolios.

"Most of those updates will merely be informing him rather than asking for complicated decisions, and they certainly won't involve starting any new projects or any new policy development, given that we're so close to the election."

Geddis acknowledged some of the criticisms that New Zealand's executive government has "an awful lot of portfolios" with ministers in charge of them, "far more so than in some other countries".

And he said some portfolios are created "almost as vanity measures", so the government can show that it is "really concerned about a particular area, without it actually needing a minister's direct oversight".

"So space seems to have been created as a portfolio mainly, so ministers can be associated with the success of the space industry."

Some of the portfolios that had fallen in Goldsmith's lap "aren't going to require much work week to week anyway", he said.

"So the fact that you can put 11 of them onto a minister and the minister is deemed able to still function, might be an indication that we simply just have too many portfolios across government as a whole."

The workload increase comes as Goldsmith has confirmed he will be campaigning for the Epsom seat, after musing momentarily that he might contest the now free Kaipara ki Mahurangi electorate, which Penk will no longer be contesting.

Epsom MP David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

Epsom MP David Seymour was pleased with Goldsmith's new workload.

"I'm very happy with him being this busy. I think it's one of the most creative and innovative ways a national leader's distracted or national candidate for Epsom."

Seymour said Goldsmith could get a lot done with minimal effort, but Goldsmith said on Wednesday it might be like a "duck swimming across water".

"It might look like its little effort, but their little legs are going frantically underneath the water."

But he has already missed one engagement, a meeting with his Australian and Japanese counterparts on his first day in the Defence role.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters suggested the issue could be resolved shortly.

"We'll take the defence portfolio. There's a defence minister in waiting. He's coming here very shortly. His name's Ron Mark."

National Minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Mark Papalii

National Minister Chris Bishop said it was not a matter of National not having enough talent to promote, but the Greens Chlöe Swarbrick suggested it was "kind of looking like" Luxon did not have anyone else he could trust to do the job.

But Luxon said he was a "safe pair of hands" and a "competent minister", with only a number of days to go before the election.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the amount of portfolios it was reasonable for a minister to have was dependent on the size of the portfolio and overall workload.

"If you're talking about Paul Goldsmith, it's ridiculous.

"Him doing all of the jobs that he's doing now, he clearly can't do justice to all of them - if you'll excuse the pun," Hipkins said about the justice minister.

"You're talking about justice, defence, broadcasting, security, and intelligence. These are big, meaty portfolios, and he's clearly not going to be able to do them justice."

World.title: Brighter economic outlook despite rising unemployment and election uncertainty
World.content:
New Zealand's economic outlook is looking brighter, despite the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, rising unemployment and uncertainty ahead of the general election.

Provisional estimates from the Infometrics June 2026 Quarterly Economic Monitor suggests economic activity rose 2.6 percent in the June 2026 quarter, and was up 1.7 percent over the year earlier.

"All 16 regional economies expanded in the June 2026 quarter," Infometrics principal economist Nick Brunsdon said.

"Growth continues to be led from the south, with Southland, Otago, Canterbury and Nelson-Tasman all growing at over 2 percent in the year to June 2026. Parts of the North Island are joining in too, with strong growth seen in both Waikato and the Bay of Plenty."

While employment growth lagged behind other economic activity, job numbers rose 0.4 percent in the June 2026 quarter, including a 0.3 percent lift in Auckland, following a decline over the past two years.

However, six regions still saw the number of jobs fall in the second quarter, with an increase in the unemployment rate and demand for work outpacing a low number of job ads.

Infometrics principal economist Nick Brunsdon. Supplied / Infometrics

"Despite the clear economic headwinds from conflict in the Middle East, economic activity might not have been as badly hit as first feared," he said.

"The more upbeat result is due to a combination of the weaker economy last year, and less of an intense hit to the economy - so far - from the Iran War."

Brunsdon said a strong primary sector and increased activity across most industries this quarter was another positive.

"That said, we remain concerned about the pace of recovery over the rest of 2026 amid continued global uncertainty."

He said household spending remained delicate, with Marketview date indicating card spending rose just 0.6 percent in the year to June 2026.

Infometrics estimates that spending volumes fell 1.5 percent over the past year, once retail inflation was accounted for, higher prices for fuel reduced the real level of spending activity.

Still, there were other positives.

"Tourism activity continues to expand, with a 3.6 percent lift in commercial guest nights recorded over the June 2026 year," Brunsdon noted.

"A 9.1 percent lift in international guest nights drove this result, as international tourism's recovery rolls on, even as domestic guest nights rose a sluggish 0.6 percent as higher fuel prices restrained Kiwi holidays across the country."

Residential construction intentions also showed recovery with a 19 percent lift to more than 40,000 building consents over the 12 months to June.

World.title: Freight industry calls for 'Minister of Supply Chain' ahead of election
World.content:
Freight operators are calling for a new government minister to lead the country's supply chains as part of their election calls.

The National Road Carriers association (NRC) is urging political parties to appoint a Minister of Supply Chain to coordinate and streamline the sector.

They said the sector was worth $59 billion a year, and was projected to grow by 55 percent over the next two decades.

"Roads sit with one minister, rail with KiwiRail, ports with councils, workforce with Immigration, and energy with another portfolio," NRC chief executive Justin Tighe-Umbers said.

He said Australia, Singapore and the United Kingdom had stronger national freight governance arrangements than New Zealand, combining ministerial oversight, dedicated government freight capability, and formal industry-government coordination mechanisms.

National Road Carriers association chief executive Justin Tighe-Umbers. Supplied / National Road Carriers

"What they [Australia, Singapore and the UK] do is they have one accountable role within their cabinet or ministerial equivalent role," Tighe-Umbers said.

"New Zealand aligns none of them," he said.

NRC's other election calls were for smarter infrastructure spending, faster adoption of international vehicle standards, stronger fuel security and support for low-emission trucks, tougher safety and licensing rules across the freight sector, and immigration settings that recognise truck driving as skilled work.

The NRC said it "appreciated" the government's recent moves, such as launching the action plan for freight, and establishing the Freight Advisory Council.

"We call on the next government to build on this momentum," Tighe-Umbers said.

On tougher safety and licensing rules, Tighe-Umbers said there were a "small but visible" number of trucking firms that were "cutting corners".

"When there's an economic downturn, obviously maintaining cashflows for operators is very difficult," he said.

"There's a small portion [of operators] when this happens, that cut corners by doing things like not maintaining their vehicles, potentially not meeting compliance ... paying for their road user charges and those sorts of things."

World.title: 'There’s been a slip': Inside the final hours before the fatal Mt Maunganui landslide
World.content:
A damning review into the fatal Mount Maunganui landslide details how one of the six victims went to extraordinary lengths to warn and help fellow campers before she was killed. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood reports.

It was day three of what was a "spur of the moment" decision by Morrinsville teacher Lisa Maclennan and her husband Travis to spend a few nights at the Beachside Holiday Park in Mount Maunganui.

They still had one more night booked, but after being woken by a slope coming down behind their campervan at about 4.30am, the couple spent the next several hours helping fellow campers and trying to alert others before deciding, at about 8.30am, that they wanted to leave.

About 9:15am, after emptying the campervan toilet receptacle, Lisa Maclennan went to have a shower in the amenities block.

Also staying at the campground were 15-year-olds Sharon Maccanico and her boyfriend Max Furse-Kee. The couple had travelled with Maccanico's parents.

Maccanico's parents had initially decided to cut the holiday short two days in following some strong windows with heavy rain predicted. However, when Maccanico's father went to cancel the remainder of their booking he was encouraged by a member of the office to stay and said they had the option of renting a caravan or a cabin.

The family decided to rent a caravan to stay in until the storm passed, when they would return to their tent.

On the morning of 22 January, the sky was blue and the family had chosen a new campsite and were ready to move.

Shortly before 9:30am, Maccanico and Furse-Kee went off to the amenities block to have showers.

Minutes later, a large landslide came down, hitting about 30 campsites and engulfing the amenities block which included toilets, showers and laundry facilities.

The six victims of the Mt Maunganui landslide - Måns Loke Bernhardsson, 20, Lisa Maclennan, 50, Susan Knowles, 71, Sharon Maccanico, 15, Max Furse-Kee, 15, and Jacqualine Wheeler, 71. Supplied

Six people were killed. They were Maclennan, Maccanico, Furse-Kee and three others who were also in the amenities block, Susan Knowles, Jacqualine Wheeler and Måns Loke Bernhardsson.

On Wednesday, an external review by retired high court judge Hon Paul Davison KSO KC, commissioned by the Tauranga City Council, was released.

The report said information identifying a risk to life was received, filed, discussed, forwarded - and then left.

"The failure was not the fault of any one person; it was the failure of a system that enabled an identified risk to life to remain unowned, un-escalated and unmanaged."

Also inside the 268-page report lies details about the "heroic lengths" Maclennan took to help those around her.

The 'spur of the moment' trip

The Maclennans arrived at the Beachside Holiday Park in the campervan they had borrowed from Lisa's family on 20 January.

At 11.57am the following day, Travis received a Civil Defence Emergency Alert on his phone.

The alert told Travis that MetService had issued a red severe rain warning for Bay of Plenty from 9am to 9am the following day.

"Put safety first. Don't take any chances. Act quickly if you see rising water. Do not try to walk, swim, or drive in floodwater.

"Avoid all non-essential travel. Bring pets indoors and move livestock to high ground where possible."

The alert also said to "be prepared to evacuate".

After returning to the campground that afternoon they remained in the campervan for the night.

About 4.30am on 22 January, Lisa woke up after hearing a noise and feeling the campervan move, the report said.

"She woke Travis who says that Lisa was panicking and initially thought that it was an earthquake.

"She went out and saw that the slope behind the campervan had come down and hit the rear of their vehicle. Some of the mud and soil from the slip had gone under the campervan covering the electric cable which was connected to a power bollard."

Lisa Maclennan, pictured with her husband Travis. NZ POLICE / SUPPLIED

Lisa moved the campervan and then woke the people who were in a blue tent that was beside them as she was worried they could be trapped if any more of the slope failed.

The report said the Maclennans wanted to "urgently" contact the management of the holiday park to tell them what had happened "so that other campers would be alerted to the risk of any further slope failures".

At 4.43am, Travis called the numbers printed on the holiday park information sheet.

The call was initially answered by a security firm who transferred him to the Tauranga City Council (TCC) contact centre.

A transcript of the call said Travis told them they were staying at the holiday park and that they were trying to get hold of them.

"There's been a slip where we're staying, and it's affected a few of us, and we obviously don't know.

"Well, we want to get hold of them so that we can let them know, but it's affected a few people here…"

He added that "a few people here need to be relocated".

The contact centre staffer asked Travis if he had tried the intercom which should put him straight to the cellphone of a person whose name is redacted in the report and named Staff Member Q.

He replied he hadn't as they were "a little bit flustered, so we rang straight through to the number, and it put us straight through to you guys".

The staffer put Travis on hold and made two calls to the campground's after-hours number, however neither call was answered.

At 4.52am the staffer called the Emergency Management Officer's (EMO) phone and spoke to a Staff Member B and transferred Travis' call to her.

Travis told Staff Member B about the slip that had come down. He said they had found the intercom which they were going to use. Staff Member B said she would get someone to call them back.

At 5.15am, Staff Member B emailed the TCC Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) operations, welfare and intelligence to tell them about two phone calls she'd had.

One was about a call she'd had from police about a slip that had taken down a house on Waitaha Road with a 10-year-old and 70-year-old missing.

The other was from Travis. She detailed what he had told her and said she'd told him she would get someone to call him back.

The report said that after his call with Staff Member B, the Maclennans tried the intercom and knocked on the walls of the campground office but had no luck.

Officials work at the scene of the landslide at the Beachside Holiday Park in Mt Maunganui on 22 January 2026. Alan Gibson / Gibson Images Ltd

They then noticed that another landslip had come down further along the driveway towards two cabins.

The couple woke the occupants of the cabins, as well as some people who were in a campervan nearby.

At 5.21am Staff Member C, who was on duty supporting the EOC controller, called Travis.

In the EOC welfare log she noted the conversation and said Travis indicated he was assisting a neighbouring camper to move their belongings.

"There had been no injuries and Travis had a location in the campground that was appropriate to shelter in place until he could raise assistance from a staff member.

"Travis was advised to call back on the EOC welfare number should he need any further support. No further calls from Travis by 7am handover."

The 111 call

The report says that at 5.47am a local resident (referred to as Member of the Public A), who had been walking near the mountain, called 111 after seeing two large landslides had come down on the ocean side near the surf club building.

His call was transferred to Fire and Emergency (FENZ) who told him that landslides were a council matter and that FENZ would notify them.

A FENZ staffer then called the TCC contact centre and told Staff Member A that they had been informed that there had been a landslide at the bottom of the mountain.

The caller had "mentioned about potentially having some problems at the Holiday Park, if the weather continues".

Member of the Public A went to the surf club to tell the lifeguards about the landslides and started waking some campers.

Staff Member A called Staff Member D, whose responsibilities included the maintenance and repair of the walkways and tracks on Mauao. He then called Staff Member F and they made a decision to immediately close all public access points onto the mountain.

Staff Member D then drove to the campground.

The Maclennans returned to the campground office several times between 5.30am and 7am to try to find someone to tell about the slips. By now, three landslips from the slope above and behind their campervan had come down.

The report said the couple also spoke with other campers.

"Travis Maclennan recalls that while he and Lisa were concerned about what had happened and thought that other campers near the base of the mountain should be warned and moved, there was no panicking."

By dawn, other campers gathered around and the couple told them why they had moved their campervan.

The couple took several photos of the slips and the blue tent, the earliest was about 6.16am.

A photograph taken by Lisa Maclennan at 6.17am on January 22. supplied

'Major slip on mount'

At 6.40am, Staff Member J, who had been alerted to the landslide by Staff Member D, sent a message to a Teams chat group used by asset managers at TCC's City Operations and Spaces and Places team.

"Major slip on mount by camp site heading [there] now to meet [Staff Member D]".

The report also referred to a Staff Member Q, who started monitoring the weather on 21 January. About 4pm he received a call advising that heavy rainfall was forecast.

During the afternoon and evening he looked out for any flooding around the holiday park.

About 11pm he called a First Security staffer asking them to keep a look out for any flooding or damage.

"He told them to contact him if there was anything to report, regardless of the time."

About 6.30am on 22 January, he woke and checked the campground's beachfront CCTV camera on his phone and saw flooding all around the beachfront campsites.

Shortly after he got a call from TCC Call Centre and was told that City Operations and other TCC staff were out in front of the campground office.

Staff Member Q went over to the ocean beachfront to see the flooding and saw that a large slip had come down and covered the stone stairs and ramp that provided access from the campground up to the base track.

When Staff Member J arrived at the campground about 6.45am, he parked his vehicle near the office and put on a hi-vis jacket.

As he approached the office he saw some people knocking on the door.

The report said Lisa asked him if he was from the campground. He replied that he was from the council.

Staff Member J said his conversation with Lisa lasted "probably two minutes".

"He described her demeanour as being frustrated and agitated because she had not been able to get hold of anybody and there was no one from the campground around to speak to."

Local emergency services search for missing people following a landslide at Mount Maunganui in Tauranga on January 23, 2026. AFP / Ben Strang

He said Lisa told him that there was a "little slip" that had hit her caravan about 4.30am.

"She said that she was worried about the bank situation where her caravan was parked … [and that] she expressed concern that people around the base of the Mount should be evacuated."

Staff Member J said he told the Maclennans that he couldn't assist them, but he would try to contact the campground manager to tell him about their concerns.

"Staff Member J is clear that Lisa was not suggesting there was any need for an urgent response by the campground management, and she was not asking him to take any urgent action in relation to either the slips or the damage caused to their campervan."

After speaking to the couple he called Staff Member N and asked them to contact Staff Member Q and get someone down to the office.

Travis said that when he and Lisa saw Staff Member Q he was speaking to some campers.

He said his wife approached Staff Member Q and said he needed to come over to their side of the campground because there had been some slips there, and they had been trying to get hold of him all morning.

Travis alleged Staff Member Q responded with what the report describes as a "rather dismissive wave of his hand" saying "I'll get there when I get there".

The couple then went back to their campervan to wait for him.

Staff Member Q's version of the conversation was different. He said he was approached by four people while he was looking at the flooding around the ocean beach campsites.

He said the Maclennans told him their camper had a bit of damage to the rear bumper.

"I said as soon as I was finished, I would come over directly to see you."

A photograph taken by Lisa Maclennan at 8.01am. supplied

Maclennans check out

At 7.37am an email was sent to the TCC executive, including the CEO and his leadership team, as well as a councillor and three other people advising them that Mount Maunganui was being closed off.

"The storm event has damaged tracks, caused slips and downed trees that make it unsafe for the public to access.

"Thankfully, as far as we know, nobody got hurt during the event."

Staff Member Q turned up at the amenities block driving the campground golf cart about 7.40am, about 40 minutes after initially speaking to the Maclennans.

Staff Member J, who was in the golf cart with Staff Member Q, said as they approached the block on the golf cart, Lisa flagged them down.

"[Staff Member J] says that Lisa appeared very concerned and said that she had been warning people near the amenities block about the potential for further slips."

Travis said Staff Member Q had offered to refund their camping charges and replace the power cable which had been covered by the landslide, and that he would get it all sorted but was going to check the rest of the area first and then come back.

The report said the Maclennans and Staff Member Q had a "different understanding" of what Staff Member Q said he was going to do.

Travis said the couple waited for him to return as they "clearly understood" that he'd said he was going to come back after checking the rest of the camp. However, Staff Member Q said he told them he would meet them at reception.

The couple ended up giving up waiting and by 8.45am they had decided they were going to check out and leave.

Travis Maclennan said when they entered the office they were surprised to see Staff Member Q was there.

He gave the couple a refund for their camping charges and a replacement electric power cable.

Davison said in his report that by now "the storm had passed, the weather had cleared and the sun was out".

"It was another classic summer morning at the Mount."

A photograph taken by Lisa Maclennan at 8.08am. supplied

Tragedy strikes

The Maclennans arrived back at their campervan about 9am and decided they would have showers before they left. Travis had one first, when he returned Lisa said she wanted the campervan toilet receptacle emptied before they left.

Given her husband had just showered she said she would do it and then go have a shower.

"Having emptied the toilet receptacle, Lisa then went into the amenities block for her shower and Mr Maclennan waited for her in the campervan. It was then around 9.15am - 9.20am."

Furse-Kee and Maccanico's family were staying in a caravan right beside the Harbour Amenities block.

Maccanico's parents woke on the morning of 22 January about 7am. Sometime before 9am, Maccanico's mum spent about 30 minutes in the amenities block washing their dishes.

When she finished she went outside and saw her daughter and Furse-Kee standing near the caravan, the report said.

"Sharon asked for the keys so that they could use the showers, and after getting some clean clothes to change into, she and Max both went off into the amenities block to have showers.

"It was now only several minutes before 9.30am."

Davison said by 9.30am the storm of the past days was "well gone".

"Many campers had either left during or after the storm, or had moved away from the low-lying and flood-affected areas of the campground, and the campground was quieter than would be usual for that time of year.

"The campsites and the driveway along the top of the campground, beneath the slope of the mountain and beside the Harbour Amenities building, appeared largely empty."

Then, about 9.30am, the slope above the amenities block "failed without any obvious warning".

"A large mass of saturated soil, colluvium, rock and debris slid rapidly down the slope. Within seconds it had engulfed the amenities building.

"Staff around the campground heard the same thing first - a loud crack, variously described as thundering or an 'almighty roar' - and then saw the trees and slope sweep down onto and over the Harbour Amenities block and campsites below."

Davison said that family members of those trapped, other campers and members of the public and TCC staff "responded immediately and made frantic efforts to locate and rescue those trapped in the building".

"It was a chaotic scene as people arrived and desperately tried to locate anyone who had been caught in the landslide."

Davison said the TCC staff "without any hesitation put themselves in danger by going onto the landslide and making desperate efforts to locate and rescue those victims caught in, or trapped by, the landslide".

"Their conduct is justly characterised and commended as being undertaken with conspicuous bravery and humanity."

Retired high court judge Hon Paul Davison KSO KC. RNZ / Kim Baker Wilson

'Warnings came early and from several directions'

Among Davison's findings, he discussed the response on the morning of the landslide.

He said Travis' call nearly five hours before the landslide was handled as a welfare and accommodation matter, not as the report of a "geohazard requiring assessment of whether the affected area should be evacuated".

Davison said Staff Member Q had no Trigger Action Response Plan to inform his decision-making and alert him to the gravity of the situation.

He also said that neither Staff Member Q or his campground staff had received any training directed to the recognition of landslide precursors such as the seepage and flow from the toe of the slopes "as become increasingly obvious during the morning of 22 January".

Davison said he made no criticism of Staff Member Q or any of the TCC staff who were present at the campground on the morning of the landslide for not recognising the signs.

"The failure to take precautionary steps to evacuate everyone from the area around and below where the fatal landslide happened on the morning of 22 January was in essence deeply systemic in origin, and the consequence of an organisational structure and risk management process that had failed to capture the natural hazard landslide risk and ensure that it was effectively assessed and managed, despite the widespread knowledge held within the organisation regarding the existence of the risk and the means of effectively mitigating it."

In the report Davison said the "central conclusion of this review is sobering in its simplicity".

"This was not a hazard that was unknown, hidden, or beyond the reach of foresight.

"For more than two decades, one competent consultant after another identified the landslide hazard to the campground, located it on the very slope that failed, and explained - sometimes in stark terms - what the consequences of a landslide occurring could be."

The slip at Mauao, Mount Maunganui as seen from the air. Screengrab / Amy Till

Davison said on the morning of 22 January, these systematic flaws combined and were compounded.

"Warnings came early and from several directions."

This included from the intense rainfall, from the large slips already coming down around the mountain, from several smaller slips on the slope, and from muddy water streaming from the foot of the slope before it finally failed.

"The instinct to move people away from the toe of the slope was even voiced by some of those who observed these signs, but there was no plan against which to assess those warnings, no threshold criteria requiring action, and no training of staff enabling them to recognise observable signs which indicated an elevated risk of slope failure and no one charged with making a properly informed evacuation decision.

"The most consequential safety decision of that morning was left, by default, to the manager at the campground who have been given neither the tools nor the knowledge to make it.

"In my view, the criticism justly and appropriately lies with the organisation that left the campground manager and his staff so ill-equipped and unprepared to make the decisions that could have avoided this tragedy."

He said had a Trigger Action Response Plan of the kind been twice recommended, that morning would have looked very different.

Following the release of the review, Travis released a statement via police.

"The council report released [on Wednesday] highlights Lisa's extraordinary and selfless actions on the morning of the landslide.

World.title: Waimakariri mayor welcomes red light on Pegasus Golf Course fast-track plan
World.content:
The Waimakariri Mayor says the decision to decline a controversial plan to rip up Canterbury's Pegasus Golf Course under fast-track approval is a wonderful win for the community.

The property developer Wolfbrook bought the 18-hole course in May and planned to redevelop the land into 1000 homes and a mixed-use commercial and community area.

Waimakariri Mayor Dan Gordon said Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop's decision not to refer the project was common sense.

"I would like to commend Minister Chris Bishop for listening to our community," he said.

Gordon said he wanted to acknowledge the "extraordinary" efforts of the Pegasus Residents Group.

"They organised, advocated, gathered more than 16,000 signatures and took their case all the way to Parliament. This result belongs first and foremost to them and the community."

However, Gordon said that the wider challenge for due process was not over.

"The proposed Ohoka development remains before fast-track, despite having already been considered and declined twice through established planning processes," he said.

Gordon said the Waimakariri District Council supported fast-track for complex projects of regional or national significance, particularly major infrastructure such as the Woodend Bypass.

World.title: Research suggests eating disorders linked to genetics, not primarily psychological
World.content:
A new international study involving University of Otago researchers links eating disorders to genetics, challenging the long-held view that they are primarily psychological illnesses.

The study was led by researchers at King's College London and the University of North Carolina and was published in the United Kingdom Journal, Nature Mental Health.

It involved analysing DNA from tens of thousands of people worldwide with binge eating or anorexia nervosa, including more than 500 New Zealand participants.

Researchers said the study provided some of the clearest evidence yet that eating disorders were influenced by both psychiatric and metabolic biology.

The study suggested that while binge eating and anorexia nervosa both fell under the category of eating disorders, they differed deeply on a biological level.

Researchers said that genetic factors associated with higher body weight were associated with an increased likelihood of binge eating.

They said that, for anorexia nervosa, the relationship was in the opposite direction, with genetic factors associated with higher body weight appearing to reduce the likelihood of developing the disorder.

The study suggested that the genetic contribution to eating disorders could not simply be explained by genes influencing body weight or body mass index (BMI).

The University of Otago Associate Professor Jenny Jordan said that represented an important shift in how eating disorders were understood and potentially treated.

"These results not only help us understand both shared and distinct causes of these eating-related traits but may also help us develop more precise treatments targeting the specific biology of each condition," she said.

World.title: Chris Bishop softens comments criticising FENZ as 'incompetent'
World.content:
National's Chris Bishop has softened comments criticising Fire and Emergency (FENZ) as "incompetent" and lacking a plan to replace a fire station, after a rebuke from the internal affairs minister.

"I was expressing frustration that the Hutt City fire station closed in 2021 and there is community concern about that," Bishop told RNZ on Wednesday.

"Five years on, little to no progress has been made. I support a proper business case and I support investment plans and asset management plans. My frustration is the delays and the lack of progress."

Internal Affairs Minister Brooke van Velden of the ACT Party had criticised his initial comments, noting that FENZ was an operationally independent crown entity.

"That means ministers can't go in and pick and choose where stations go, but FENZ needs to identify which areas need investment the most," she said.

"We have a forecast for 10 years to spend at least $700 million on property investment across New Zealand, and in the next financial year, about 30 different stations up and down New Zealand will see investment into those areas.

"I don't want to see this being politicised, because it is a Crown entity that does make operationally independent decisions. It really isn't up to me or any other minister, or it shouldn't be, that in an election campaign we promise stations in certain areas."

Bishop had made the initial comments at a public meeting in Lower Hutt on Tuesday when asked about the station's closure.

A member of the public had asked why - given Labour sorted union negotiations out with fire-fighters after the first ever nation-wide strike - National had not done the same after 54; and why a community centre burned down about 550 metres from the previous fire station that got shut down.

"Been multiple fires in Alicetown, including the devastating local fire at the community centre on the 5th of November '25. It's approximately 550 metres from the old station - that should have been a fire extinguisher on the deck, put out within a minute.

"That building, sadly, was so badly damaged it's now been demolished, and the local community doesn't have a community centre."

Bishop said the problem was "emblematic of everything wrong with the way we do infrastructure in New Zealand".

"FENZ is a shocker at managing their assets. They barely know what they own. They don't have a long-term asset management plan for building new stuff like replacing fire stations that they need to close down.

"I have been pushing them and the Minister of Internal Affairs Brooke van Velden very hard to say 'what is the plan around the Hutt City fire station', and I just get crickets in response because you've got an incompetent governance and management there who've got no idea what they're doing and the Hutt is being let down, and I'm furious about it."

The infrastructure minister, Bishop said National would "keep pushing hard on that because we do need a new fire station there ... I'm sick of being told 'oh, we're working on a business case, we're working on this'. It's blah blah blah blah blah. It's all just blah blah blah. We need action."

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon had followed up, responding to the question about union negotiations by noting that was meant to be a process independent of ministerial involvement.

He said the FENZ management team "has collected a huge amount of revenue off the back of corporate levies off commercial buildings, and has had plenty of money and has done dumb things with it".

"The bottom line is... they have money. They have enough money. You think about the value of commercial property in New Zealand and how that has risen over the last 10 years and what they have done with it is some really dumb stuff."

Luxon said they were "thinking very clearly about FENZ", and would be "socialising" a number of them "so just hang fire".

"You know, we've got an Emergency Manager Minister, but doesn't have responsibility for- ... there's a whole bunch of just mush in the middle of it all."

FENZ told RNZ Lower Hutt had the same number of fire-fighters responding to emergencies as it always had.

"We moved our people to Avalon because their previous building wasn't safe," the organisation said.

"Operational requirements for Hutt City will be approved by the end of September, and a business case is underway. That work tells us what's needed, where, and what it costs.

"We are considering an interim facility in the meantime. We have been searching for a site throughout. None have met our needs."

Van Velden said it was "no secret that FENZ has long-standing issues".

"I have been focussed on addressing them after years of neglect. I have directed the Board and chief executive to focus on strong planning and management of assets going forward, and finding back-office savings to re-invest in the front line.

"Under my watch, they have now completed a full suite of Asset Management Plans across its key operational areas, including Fleet, Property, ICT and Equipment. This is a massive improvement on where they were under previous governments."

World.title: Urgent debate or urgent farewell: MPs discuss Chris Penk
World.content:
Tuesday's urgent parliamentary debate on Chris Penk's demotion was about a fairly specific topic: the prime minister's decision to remove one of his ministers from Cabinet for disloyalty. In practice, it was a rather more eclectic collection of reckons from around the House. At times it resembled a fond farewell tribute.

Urgent debate or urgent farewell: MPs debate demotion of Chris Penk The House Download MP3 5m

There was the expected political crossfire over the events of the previous week. Labour argued it exposed deeper problems for Christopher Luxon's leadership. National MPs' responses were tantamount to "nothing to see here", instead aiming to spotlight Labour's hypothetical tax policies. But there were also more personal interpretations of the situation.

ACT's Simon Court used a decent portion of his contribution to lament the end of Penk's ministerial tenure, and praise Penk's work in the Building and Construction portfolio. He tucked in some campaigning too. Court is standing in Penk's electorate and hoping some of Penk's supporters might jump into the ACT waka instead of the National one as a protest or proxy vote.

Simon Court praises Chris Penk and then makes a plea for voters to choose him as Penk's replacement during an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk. VNP / Phil Smith

Court's praise contrasted with the political argument surrounding Penk's removal. At times the debate sounded less like a dispute over a ministerial decision and more like a valedictory for someone who had already left.

Te Pāti Māori's Debbie Ngarewa-Packer and Labour's Carmel Sepuloni both went out of their way to acknowledge the now former minister personally, describing him in warm terms as an "honourable man" who was "here for the right reasons", and praising the way he conducted himself across the House.

Te Pāti Māori leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer during an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge. VNP / Phil Smith

Te Pāti Māori's Debbie Ngarewa-Packer described Penk as "one of the better human beings on that side".

Former National Party leader Judith Collins appears to enjoy an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge. VNP / Phil Smith

Almost the only party not to praise the fallen minister was his own party. As speeches ping-ponged back and forth between the two major parties, the very short contributions from National MPs largely stuck to the party line: Penk acted alone, actions have consequences, and it was time to move on.

Then there was Kieran McAnulty, who praised Penk but focused on picking apart attempts by various National MPs to draw a line under the events.

Kieran McAnulty dissects the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge. VNP / Phil Smith

Through all of this, there were two notable absences - both the demoter and the demoted.

Christopher Luxon's seat remains empty during an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge against him. VNP / Phil Smith

Chris Penk isn't at Parliament this week, and was not in the House to explain his actions, or respond to the various assessments of his character and political judgment. The prime minister had departed the House prior to the end of Question Time; his actions as well as Penk's were debated without him. The one minister present who was discussed was Erica Stanford, who sat still and silent, like a pupil sent to await the headmaster.

Ultimately, the House's traversal of last week's political melodrama was a forum for criticism, defence, campaigning and a fond farewell from the most unexpected quarters, missing only its protagonists.
