World.title: 'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident
World.content:
Five Sydney Swans players who were stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards have issued an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

In a statement on behalf of Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner, the players said they were "deeply sorry to everyone involved".

The players were banned by the Swans for breaches of standards and expected behaviour after they stayed out late drinking and brought women back to the team hotel after the game against Essendon on Sunday night.

"We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club," they said.

The five said that they accepted the club's sanction and apologised for the impact on those involved.

Earlier in the day, the Swans said their willingness to "torpedo" their AFL season by suspending the five star players proved their commitment to upholding standards at the club.

In addition to the club sanction, the five Swans players will not be considered for All Australian selection, according to the AFL.

"Following the decision and appropriate club sanction imposed by the Sydney Swans today in relation to the conduct of five of their players, the AFL has determined those players will not be considered for selection in the 2026 All Australian squad," the league said in a statement.

"This decision is independent of the ongoing Victoria Police investigation."

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich (left) and chairman Andrew Pridham. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Victorian detectives head to NSW

Victorian sex crime detectives are expected to travel to New South Wales as they investigate the alleged incident.

The ABC understands the investigation centres on an allegation of touching without consent at the Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

It is understood the alleged victim has spoken to police.

Multiple law enforcement sources have told the ABC that four officers from the Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad will land in Sydney as they expand their investigation.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges over the alleged incident.

It is not suggested that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault, and none of the banned players has been formally interviewed by police, according to the club.

Sponsors speak out

Telstra has spoken out, saying it was "deeply concerned by what's been reported" and respected that the matter was being investigated by police.

"Players assisting police with their investigation who are also Telstra ambassadors are not participating in any ambassador activity while the investigation is ongoing," a Telstra spokesperson said.

"We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time."

It is understood that Heeney and Warner have both been Telstra ambassadors.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

Swans sponsors QBE came out in support of the club's actions.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson said today.

"We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club's position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women.

"Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further."

Another club sponsor, realestate.com.au, also responded, saying they were "deeply concerned about the serious allegations involving several Sydney Swans players".

"We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations," a company spokesperson said.

Swans sanctions solely for breaches of club standards

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich have stressed the decision to ban the players is solely related to breaches of the club's standards and expected behaviour.

"Hopefully people can see how seriously we've taken this matter," Pridham said.

"We're very proud of our culture we've built over many years at the club. We get more right than we get wrong. Clearly this is a very sad day for us and for everybody involved.

"I know the five players involved, they're extremely remorseful for their actions in breaching the club's standards, and I think the sanction we've imposed and the impact that will have on our football season is clear for all to see.

"It's very important to note the football outcome was not a consideration of the board."

Loading...

Sydney's sanctions came after the club conducted interviews with the players linked to the Melbourne incident off-site with their lawyers present. Sydney's board met on Tuesday night to discuss club-imposed sanctions.

The bans handed to the players, according to the club bosses, relate to their decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women back to the hotel.

Pavlich said it fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players", and Pridham added that their actions left the club with no choice but to impose a heavy sanction.

"They shouldn't have been in that situation," Pridham said.

"The only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we've done. To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this tells you how seriously we're taking this."

The AFL has backed the team's sanctions and the Swans say their decision is independent of an ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The rest of the Swans will prepare for North Melbourne on Sunday and then a finals campaign. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The players' ban includes this Sunday's home-and-away finale against North Melbourne and any finals matches the Swans will play afterwards.

Pavlich said the club was "deeply embarrassed and ashamed", stressing they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare and wellbeing of the women involved.

"They're the ones who are impacted severely at the moment," he said, adding that the Swans did not want to interfere with the police investigation by reaching out to the women directly.

While the five suspended players will not be allowed to play for the rest of the year, Pavlich said "they will be allowed back at the football club" this season.

"We're not abandoning our players," he said.

"We are supporting our players through this really challenging time for them."

Pridham pointed out the sanctions should not tarnish the entire team's reputation.

"There are many players this doesn't apply to, and I believe our male team has, by and large, displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something of concern," he said.

"However, clearly when situations such as this emerge, and clearly there has been a breakdown in standards, we will, in time, as a board and as an executive team, review how we deal with these things going forward and we'll look to see if changes need to be made.

"We're very, very proud of our culture. We don't get everything perfectly right over time, and things happen from time to time, and it's how we fix it going forward."

West Coast AFLW head coach Daisy Pearce has called on men to "be a good human" not just for themselves but for the effect they have on others. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

AFLW pioneer Daisy Pearce says it is "disappointing" allegations of violence against women have arisen again in the AFL.

Speaking at a press conference, West Coast Eagles AFLW coach Pearce urged young men to consider how their behaviour impacted others.

"Be a good human. Be a good human and for those that are in high-profile positions understand that you being a good human matters but it also has a massive impact on what other people think is acceptable as well," she said.

World.title: Ikitau back in fray as Wallabies eye Argentina tour
World.content:
Les Kiss has resisted throwing any curveballs ahead of the Wallabies' tour of Argentina, with a fit Len Ikitau the only addition to the squad that produced wins in his first two Tests as coach.

Ikitau (ankle), the 2025 Wallabies player of the year, had minor surgery and missed the recent victories against Japan in Osaka and Townsville.

He has effectively replaced unlucky fullback Jock Campbell, who impressed in the number 15 jersey against Ireland before injuries elsewhere saw him employed as a play-making bench option against France.

With Tom Wright locked in at fullback, Campbell, who was named the Queensland Reds' best player at this week's end-of-season awards, was replaced by Ben Donaldson as the fullback or fly half bench cover for the next three Tests.

Les Kiss seeking pride The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Centre Josh Flook has also been left out while Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii (hamstring) will also return after missing Saturday's Townsville Test, creating a log-jam of midfield options against the world number seven Pumas.

Winger Max Jorgensen has been included despite coming off with a sore chest on Saturday, while code-hopper Zac Lomax remains on the injury list and unavailable for selection.

Lock Miles Amatosero, unavailable for the first Test as part of a three-game suspension for a red card earned in Osaka, was also not considered for selection.

Kiss, who tested new combinations in the pack and centres in his first two games in charge, has otherwise played a straight bat ahead of what will be sterner tests in San Salvador de Jujuy and Mendoza on August 30 and September 6.

"As coaches, we've looked to maintain consistency in selection, with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks through their hard work and connection on and off the field," he said.

"Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it's one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game."

Where Kiss selects Suaalii will be telling after Isaac Henry's strong running and second-phase play at outside centre caught the eye in Townsville.

Hunter Paisami has also impressed at number 12 in Ikitau's absence, leading to questions post-match about where Suaalii fits in the picture.

There is a push for former NRL star Suaalii to move to the wing to ensure more involvement and better harness his aerial ability.

Kiss, who replaced Joe Schmidt ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup, said before his first Test in charge that he was "persisting at number 13 with him at this stage, but I know that he can go to fullback and wing, and that's important to acknowledge as well".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But Campbell and Flook's exclusion from this squad hints that Kiss is now considering a Suaalii switch.

Zane Nonggorr (calf) remains sidelined, with Massimo De Lutiis set for his first full Wallabies tour after arriving late into Osaka and debuting in Townsville.

Wright will notch 50 Test caps if he plays in both Tests.

The squad will assemble in Sydney on Saturday, before departing for Buenos Aires on Sunday.

World.title: Germany star says neurological issue behind two collapses in a week
World.content:
Bayern Munich midfielder Jamal Musiala has revealed a neurological issue but says he is doing well despite collapsing during a preseason game for the second time in a week.

The 23-year-old Germany international went down shortly after entering Wednesday's (AEST) friendly as a substitute in the second half. Players from both teams made a circle around Musiala as he received medical treatment. He was then helped as he walked off the pitch.

Musiala had collapsed Sunday (AEST) during a friendly against Leipzig. German news agency DPA reported he had left the field on his own but still appeared dazed.

After Wednesday's game, Musiala posted a message on his Instagram account, explaining that he had been diagnosed with temporary "but easily treatable absence seizures" caused by a neurological problem.

"These can lead to the moments that happened recently, such as against Leipzig or even now in Heidenheim," Musiala wrote.

Bayern, in its report on Wednesday's game, only said of the incident: "There was a setback when Jamal Musiala had to be subbed off with a knock minutes after coming on."

Jamal Musiala was held up by teammate Ismael Saibari (left) after fainting during Bayern's friendly against RB Leipzig. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

Musiala said he was "very optimistic" and was receiving excellent medical treatment.

"The important thing is that there is no additional health risk," he wrote.

"In close coordination and regular communication with experts, it has been my personal wish to face the challenge and, with the endorsement of the neurological specialists, to devote myself to what helps me most in recovery: to simply live my everyday life and keep up with my passion of playing football," Musiala added.

Bundesliga champion Bayern faces Borussia Dortmund on Sunday AEST in the German Supercup, the traditional curtain-raiser for the season.

AP

World.title: Irankunda says Hanson's monoculture comments upset team during World Cup
World.content:
Socceroos star winger Nestory Irankunda says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's comments on multiculturalism upset many of the players during the recent World Cup.

The Australian team was competing at the tournament in North America in June when Ms Hanson made a speech at the National Press Club saying Australia should end its policy of multiculturalism in favour of a monoculture.

"It really did upset me and it upset a lot of the other boys to see things and hear things like that," Irankunda said.

" I felt a bit emotional but then tried to forget about it. "

Irankunda, who is one of several Socceroos players from a refugee background, told 702 ABC Sydney while he tried to stay off social media it was hard to avoid the senator's comments.

Loading...

"There can be some people who do the wrong thing but that doesn't mean that's all of us," he said.

"There's people like me, and Awer [Mabil], Mohamed Touré that go out there. There's a lot of boys like us that go out there and do the right thing.

"I don't like how they try and put us in the whole same category as the other people who do bad."

Irankunda was born in a refugee camp in Tanzania in 2006 to Burundian parents who fled the nation's civil war. He came to Australia when he was three months old.

Irankunda was speaking with presenter Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney just days after moving from English Championship club Watford to Portuguese side Sporting CP for an undisclosed fee reported to be in the region of $26 million.

The footballer said he probably wouldn't like to speak with the One Nation senator as he was still upset by the comments and "some of the things she said in the past".

"I'm not someone that likes to jump into controversial things or this political stuff. But I mean, you know, you never know," Irankunda said.

"One day I could be on the phone with her or sitting in an office chatting to her. So I mean … we'll see what happens."

Pauline Hanson's speech at the National Press Club included a call to end Australia's decades-old policy of multiculturalism. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

After her press club speech, Hanson said the Socceroos represented her vision of a monocultural Australia.

"People from different background and cultures and nations all wearing the green and gold and representing one nation under one flag and succeeding under the same set of rules," Hanson said in the Senate in June.

Socceroo Awer Mabil addressed the monoculture debate when he returned in July from the tournament, declaring his team was not distracted and that it was "all bullshit" to suggest Australia was not a multicultural society.

Australian team destined to 'go far'

Irankunda said despite the Round of 32 loss to Egypt, the Socceroos had youth on their side and could go further into the tournament.

"You can see now with the likes of Lucas Herrington, Ali [Alessandro] Circati, Jordy Bos, you know, Mohamed Touré, all these names, all these young boys coming through, including myself," Irankunda said.

"There's still a lot of talent coming through in Australia right now.

"Only time will tell how far we can go. But I feel like in my heart that we can go pretty far."

World.title: FIFA accused of 'management by fear' after key executive's sudden exit
World.content:
The head of Norwegian football has accused FIFA of fear tactics for the removal of a senior official who publicly opposed FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-withdrawn World Cup sell-off plan.

Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian Football Federation since 2022, told the Associated Press that the firing of FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour was "unacceptable" and urged other senior leaders to resist potentially damaging orders.

Mr Lamour's exit on Tuesday (AEST) came 17 days after his statement to AP criticising Mr Infantino's $US20 billion ($28.1 billion) private equity project, which was withdrawn hours later.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"Now he is thrown out and we are supposed to move on. It's unacceptable, it's management by fear," Ms Klaveness told the AP in a telephone interview, describing Mr Lamour as "the best football administrator I have ever met".

"Now we also have to call upon FIFA leadership and the administration to not submit to orders you know are not in the interests of football," Ms Klaveness added, especially targeting FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafström.

Ms Klaveness represented Norway 73 times as a player, is a judge in Oslo and an elected executive committee member at European football body UEFA.

She has built on her country's long-held reputation as a champion of good governance in soccer.

Last week the Norwegian federation's board called on Mr Infantino to resign and has backed a London-based NGO's formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators about his political ties to US President Donald Trump.

Mr Lamour was a long-time colleague of Mr Infantino, first when they were senior officials at UEFA from 2007-15. He was involved in Mr Infantino's campaign to be elected FIFA president in 2016 and moved two years ago from UEFA to oversee much of FIFA's operations in Zurich.

Infantino in crisis

Kevin Lamour (centre) said FIFA staff were "deceived" by the World Cup sell-off plan. (Getty Images: Richard Sellers)

With a reputation among the most trusted executives in the often murky world of global football politics, Mr Lamour's pointed criticisms of Mr Infantino's leadership intensified a crisis for the FIFA president.

A backlash from UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and north American soccer body CONCACAF was provoked by a secretive plan to sell future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

A $4.2 billion investment to take a 20 per cent stake in a FIFA commercial spin-off was to fund offers of $20 million to each of its 211 national member federations.

They already effectively own the non-profit soccer body, which has multi-billion dollar reserves, and would have had a mid-September deadline to accept.

Mr Lamour's statement on July 31 spoke of FIFA staff being "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness over the now-failed sale and how they "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

The French executive called on soccer leaders worldwide "to make the right decisions".

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he said at the conclusion of the statement.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

'A firing situation'

Lise Klaveness with Gianni Infantino at last month's FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

Ms Klaveness said Mr Lamour's exit was "a firing situation, it's not a resignation", and suggested it was done as a result of Mr Grafström "obviously being pressured by the president".

FIFA didn't respond to a request for comment on Ms Klaveness's remarks.

In a statement, FIFA said it "thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter".

Mr Lamour did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on Wednesday (AEST).

"His statement was necessary to kill the project," Ms Klaveness said of Mr Lamour's intervention.

" He said something that was obvious, that was very important that someone within the staff told us the story so that we knew it was not FIFA, as such, but one person. "

Mr Infantino held a meeting with senior management — minus Mr Lamour — in Rabat, Morocco on August 5.

Following that, FIFA issued a statement apologising for errors and said those managers who attended "reaffirmed their full support" for Mr Infantino's presidency.

"We all got reports in Morocco, we know it's a management of fear," Ms Klaveness said.

"It's not in football's best interests."

Until the uproar over Mr Infantino's "FIFA Forward Enterprise" proposal, he seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next year in Morocco for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

Challengers have until November 18 to enter the contest.

Norway not discussing other candidates

Though UEFA and other critics of Mr Infantino want him ousted from the $6 million-per-year FIFA job, Ms Klaveness said any search for an opponent was not a talking point in Norway.

"We are not there at all and that is 100 per cent the truth," she said, adding that any candidate would have to be "very accountable to a governance structure that will not in four or five years just deteriorate".

Mr Infantino was appointed by UEFA in 2015 to a panel advising FIFA on reforms, in fallout from corruption scandals provoked by US federal investigations.

That group's recommendations limiting FIFA presidents to 12 years in office, plus limiting their executive powers and patronage all have retreated under Mr Infantino.

Ms Klaveness acknowledged FIFA members had been less "passionate about the details of governance" than Norway.

Mr Lamour also won praise and support from UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister, also a former player and now a university professor of governance in Wales, who lamented the "shabby events of the past weeks".

"Kevin's sacking seriously weakens FIFA's administration whilst undermining this unique opportunity to shift the culture at FIFA and to reset the organisation on sporting values, not simply commercial and financial ones," Ms McAllister said.

AP

World.title: Dees star's ban upheld as AFL tribunal rejects biomechanist evidence bid
World.content:
Melbourne has suffered a major pre-finals blow, potentially losing key forward Jacob van Rooyen for the rest of the AFL season through suspension.

The Demons failed in their bid to have van Rooyen's three-game ban for striking overturned or reduced.

It means he will miss the fifth-placed Demons' final home-and-away game on Saturday against the Western Bulldogs, and that Melbourne will need to win two finals for him to play again this season.

Van Rooyen is having a career-best season, kicking 42 goals in 22 games.

The Demons forward was charged with striking after he concussed Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir in a marking contest on Saturday night at the Adelaide Oval. It was graded as severe impact, careless conduct and high impact.

After the 90-minute hearing, where van Rooyen testified that he was trying to mark the ball when he collected Aliir, the tribunal jury deliberated for nearly an hour before upholding the charge.

Melbourne had argued van Rooyen's attempt to mark the ball was not careless, but the tribunal rejected their case.

Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC also turned down a bid from the Demons to have a biomechanist give evidence for van Rooyen.

Aliir Aliir was left concussed after being struck in the head by van Rooyen's swinging arm. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

"The swing of van Rooyen's left arm constituted the act of a strike. It was a forceful blow. It was not simply a trailing or leading arm that Aliir collided with," Gleeson said in the verdict, adding the panel found it was careless.

"Van Rooyen was initially intending to mark the ball, but we find that shortly before impact, he ceased to intend to mark the ball. We say this despite van Rooyen's evidence to the contrary.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Even if it was van Rooyen's sole objective at all times to contest the mark, we find that he did so in a way that failed to take reasonable care to avoid acts which could be reasonably foreseen to result in a reportable offence.

"Van Rooyen had time to move his right arm in response to seeing Aliir and he could have done so to some extent or sufficient extent with his left arm."

The tribunal also found the impact was severe and said there was potential for further injury, such as a facial fracture.

Also on Tuesday night, Brisbane AFLW key forward Dakota Davidson failed to have her one-game striking ban downgraded.

The Lions pleaded guilty and tried to argue the clash with Essendon's Maddi Gay was low rather than medium impact, but the AFLW tribunal upheld the grading.

It means one of the league's top forwards will miss the grand final rematch against two-time defending premiers North Melbourne.

AAP

World.title: Venus Williams receives US Open wildcard at 46, Serena may follow
World.content:
Venus Williams has received a US Open singles wild card and the tournament is keeping one on hold, perhaps in case her sister Serena wants to join her.

Sloane Stephens, the 2017 US Open champion, was one of six other women to receive a wild card, and the US Tennis Association said the final one was still to be announced.

That will almost certainly go to Serena Williams if she decides she wants to return to the tournament at 44.

Venus Williams received a wild card last year, returning to the grand slam event she won twice for the first time since 2023. The 46-year-old has become the oldest entrant in singles at the tournament since Renee Richards played at 47 in 1981, according to the International Tennis Federation.

Serena Williams could make her return to Flushing Meadows via the final wildcard spot. (Getty Images: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport)

She has continued to play some singles matches, and this week joined Serena for their first doubles tournament together since the 2022 US Open. They lost at the Cincinnati Open in a match tiebreaker against Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns.

The sisters planned to play at Wimbledon but had to withdraw after Serena injured her knee in her singles match. That marked her first time playing singles since the 2022 US Open, and she indicated afterwards that she hoped to keep competing if she was healthy.

Headlining the wild-card recipients on the men's side are 39-year-old Gael Monfils, a past US Open semifinalist who is set to play his final grand slam tournament before retiring, and Australian Alexei Popyrin, who upset Novak Djokovic in 2024 on the way to the fourth round.

One spot is also being held among the eight men's wild cards. Stan Wawrinka, the 2016 champion at Flushing Meadows, who at 41 is playing his final season, could be a candidate for that.

Australia's Alexei Popyrin has received one of the wildcards in the men's draw. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/David Kirouac)

Also receiving women's wild cards were Carol Young Suh Lee, Reese Brantmeier, Thea Frodin, Leolia Jeanjean and Taylah Preston.

The other men receiving wild cards were two-time reigning NCAA singles champion Michael Zheng, Martin Damm, JJ Wolf, Sebastian Gorzny and Jack Kennedy.

Kei Nishikori, the 2014 US Open runner-up who also is retiring, was given a wild card into the men's qualifying tournament, along with Jordan Lee, Trevor Svajda, Andre Ilagan, Spencer Johnson, Michael Antonius, Andrew Johnson and Daniel Milavsky.

Women given spots in the qualifying tournament were Caroline Dolehide, Janae Preston, Katrina Scott, Ayana Akli, Annika Penickova, Julieta Pareja, Kristina Penickova and Savannah Broadus.

The main draw begins on August 30, with the qualifying tournaments being played earlier that week.

AP

Tech.title: GTA VI keeps leaking ahead of its gameplay premiere
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Clips of what appears to be Grand Theft Auto VI have hit the internet, possibly spoiling aspects of the game ahead of Rockstar Games’ deep dive debuting on Netflix next week and its long-awaited launch in November.

I’ve seen three clips seemingly showing off the game, though two have been pulled from the site I saw them on “due to a copyright claim.” The first clip (now removed) was a quiet scene that mostly focused on Jason Duval, one the game’s two protagonists, shooting a basketball into a hoop. Another clip (also removed) featured more of the crime-focused gameplay you’d expect from GTA, including Duval hitting a person with a wrench, and also showed the return of a six-star Wanted system.

A third clip, which is live as I write this, shows Duval driving at night, punching some people, using a taser, and stealing a truck. The clip then jumps to what looks like a cutscene from a different part of the game in the daytime.

The videos were watermarked by a person or group identifying themselves as “CyberLeek.” The third clip has a call for viewers to buy a CyberLeek cryptocurrency, a QR code, links to some sketchy-looking CyberLeek URLs, and a statement that says “NO PHYSICAL DISCS? THEN MORE LEEKS!”, which is seemingly a reference to Rockstar’s decision not to launch GTA VI on a physical disc.

This isn’t the first time apparent footage from GTA VI has leaked. In 2022, 90 videos leaked online long before the game’s official reveal more than a year later (a reveal that also leaked, leading Rockstar to publish the game’s first trailer a day early). A teen who played a key role in leaking the 90 videos was sentenced to life in a secure hospital. Rockstar also confirmed earlier this year that it had data compromised in a hack of a third-party provider, but said the incident would have “no impact on our organization or our players.”

Rockstar and owner Take-Two didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. The GTA VI “extended look” premieres on Netflix on August 27th at 3PM ET and will stream on YouTube at 9PM ET. The $79.99 title is scheduled to launch on November 19th, and for the most part, the industry is steering clear of November and launching their big games earlier in the year.

Tech.title: Meta AI is getting a Mac app
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta is launching a new Mac app dedicated to its AI chatbot. In an announcement on Wednesday, Meta says you can share your window with its AI chatbot, which can provide suggestions, answer questions, or create content based on what’s on your screen. Meta AI on the Mac also supports dictation across all apps.

The launch comes as Meta makes its AI chatbot more like a productivity-focused assistant to better compete with its AI rivals — many of which already have desktop apps. You can share your window with Google’s Gemini AI app, while OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude apps take things a step further by allowing the chatbots to take control of your computer.

You can use Meta AI for dictation across other apps as well. GIF: Meta

Along with the new app, Meta is introducing new AI capabilities for businesses and creators. The company says its app across the web, on mobile, and on Mac can now work directly with Instagram and Facebook accounts, Meta ad campaigns, and Google Workspace.

As an example, Meta says its AI chatbot can analyze the reach of posts, along with their likes, shares, and saves, to make suggestions about what to post next. The app can also pull information from a business’s account and the web to create decks, docs, and spreadsheets, as well as perform recurring tasks, like providing weekly performance updates.

The embargo has lifted on Google’s Pixel 11 series, as well as for its Pixel Watch 5. Now we get to talk smack — just kidding, the new hardware is good. We can’t stop you from asking irrelevant questions, but we’ll be prioritizing ones that are focused on Google hardware and the new features (Camera Looks, Creator Suite, Magic Capture, Proactive Assistance, and so on), our experiences with the products during testing, who they’re for, and who might be able to skip on this year’s models. If you ask us to try Proactive Assistance with a specific example, we might just comply.

Tech.title: The Pixel 11 Pro is a great phone, no thanks to its flashiest new features
Tech.content:
is a technology reporter who has been covering the industry since 2007. He co-hosts the Waveform podcast with MKBHD. A former engineer, he now specializes in topics like computational photography and social media protocols.

Google is trying to get you off your phone. The Pixel 11 Pro is “A Phone Designed to Help You Use It Less,” the company promises. It can proactively help you book restaurant reservations, take the best frames from a video, and help you voice-text significantly faster. The pitch is that the new features bundled with the Pixel 11 series of phones can help fix your relationship with technology — one that Google knows has badly degraded in recent years.

But the hardware of the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL is very similar to last year’s models — and in at least one case, a downgrade — so those software features are pretty much the entire pitch.

Over the last week testing the 11 Pro, I’ve been trying them all to see how much they can help me put my phone down. Like many experiences with Google software, when they work, they are genuinely helpful. But getting them to work often requires a very narrow set of circumstances that some Google engineer probably dreamed up in the “society if” utopia lab.

The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL are minor hardware updates compared to last year’s Pixel 10 Pro and 10 Pro XL. They both get brighter 3,600-nit screens. Their charging has been upgraded, with faster wired speeds and Qi2.2 for up to 25W when wireless. The 5x optical telephoto camera has a bigger sensor that Google says enables 30 percent more light intake. Storage now starts at 256GB, instead of 128GB. And there’s also a fancy new “notification light,” which I’ll get to in a bit.

Unfortunately, these upgrades come with a downgrade too, for the base model at least. The 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL now start with less RAM: 12GB compared to the 16GB that came standard last year, the same amount as the regular Pixel 11. I’m testing the 16GB / 512GB model, so unfortunately I can’t tell you if the RAM decrease is noticeable. That base model is also $100 more expensive than last year, too, at $1,099.

With such minor spec changes, Google has gone all in on software this year. And this time, that software’s primary purpose is to get you off your phone, or at least get tedious tasks done faster so you can get back to your life.

Proactive Assistance popping up inside Google Messages.

Perhaps the largest push in this direction is the Pixel 11’s new “Proactive Assistance” feature. This is a set of dynamic chips that appear when certain interactions happen on your phone, like a friend asking what your schedule looks like next week or if you booked that table at a restaurant yet.

For the most basic interactions, like checking availability or adding an event to my calendar, I found Proactive Assistance really helpful. I practically live inside my calendar, and text conversations about scheduling are common. When my friend Marc texted me asking when I was available next week, Gemini popped up and suggested checking my calendar for times. Outside of simple scenarios like that, though, Proactive Assistance gets less reliable. One of Google’s key examples is letting Gemini book a dinner reservation for you if you’re chatting about heading out to eat, but I had to receive a text with an extremely specific string of information to get it to work — and even then it only worked sometimes.

It’s odd that explicit keywords are necessary to get so much of Proactive Assistance to work

For example, receiving the text “Can you make a reservation at Frankie Spuntino next Saturday at 7pm?” surfaced a chip to agentically try to make the reservation. But if the message doesn’t include the date or time, it won’t invoke anything at all. Most of the time when the chip does show up, it disappears the moment I reply. Occasionally it will stick around if the AI thinks we’re still talking about the restaurant, but those instances were few and far between. I wish Google would keep the chip around for at least a few messages, or have it float around the messages in some way.

One promise of large language models is the ability to understand what you mean and remove the requirements for smart keywords, so it’s odd that explicit keywords are still necessary to get so much of Proactive Assistance to work. I can see what Google is trying to do with this and I can maybe see a future where it gets refined, but as it stands, it’s simply too inconsistent. Plus, I had to manually toggle on Proactive Assistance and add OpenTable to connected apps in settings, which I just don’t think most people will know to do. As my colleague Cameron Faulkner puts it, “You need to be proactive to get Proactive Assistance to work.”

Proactive Assistance is advertised as working with other scenarios too, like surfacing your flight information when someone asks what time your flight is or bringing up the right photo when someone asks for it. But both of these scenarios either failed or were inconsistent for me. Asking when my flight is supposed to land surfaced nothing even though I have flight information in my Gmail, and when my friend asked for a photo of me from 2024, it surfaced photos from 2024, but none of me. It’s disappointing that this feature only works in such narrow circumstances. I can see the vision, but the execution just isn’t there yet.

The HiLight LED.

Another feature that got a lot of marketing hype but flatlined on its delivery is HiLight. You may have noticed the temperature sensor is missing on the Pixel 11 Pro. Instead, Google has replaced it with a multicolored LED ring hidden inside the flash that can glow when different things are happening on your phone. Again, in concept, I love this idea. Google wants you to be living your life, with your phone placed face down on the table so it can’t distract you unless HiLight notifies you of something you need to pay attention to. In practice, HiLight is so badly executed that it’s frankly embarrassing.

Right now, HiLight can glow for exactly two things. First, it will glow and animate when you’re speaking with Gemini, but only while your phone is face down on the table. These are two things I do not do very often. When I use Gemini, I’m generally typing to it, and when I do use Gemini voice mode, my phone is in my hand or sitting screen up. If this was just one of the many things HiLight could light up for, I wouldn’t find it so offensive. But at the moment, the only other thing HiLight will glow for is for calls from your favorite contacts. I wish I was kidding.

The only options for HiLight.

If I’m getting a call from a favorite contact, I just want my phone to ring. Again, if it was just an additional feature, then sure, I guess. I don’t mind having an additional indicator that a favorite is calling me while my phone is face down. But if the call is coming through anyway, it’s really not that much effort to turn the phone over and see who it is. To make it worse, you can only choose from five colors, and one of them is white!

Customizable RGB LEDs were a feature we lost long ago, but when we did have it, it was almost always possible to map to just about any notification you wanted: red for a new email, green for a WhatsApp message. Google has confirmed that it’s looking to add text notifications from favorite contacts to HiLight, but why not just make it customizable to any app? This feels like such a missed opportunity, and it’s wild to me that it wasn’t better thought out before launch. Right now, it’s just acting like my flash, like it’s always been.

There are some new features that I’m finding genuinely useful that do help me stay in the moment, though. I was most pleasantly surprised by Rambler, a souped-up voice-to-text tool powered by Gemini. Rambler removes the filler words that voice-to-text would normally pick up, does proper grammar and punctuation without explicitly asking for it, and will even rewrite misspeaks mid-recording. The speed of the Pixel’s voice-to-text has been one of its strong suits ever since Google started using its own Tensor chips on the Pixel 6, but Rambler makes this even better, to the point where I’m dictating the text on my phone whenever I have the opportunity. It is a genuinely great feature, saves me time, and almost makes it feel like I’m having a conversation in real time while texting.

Using Rambler on the Pixel 11 Pro.

As is tradition, Google also introduced a bunch of new camera features this year, and perhaps the most prominent is Magic Capture. The feature is front and center in the camera app right next to the photo and video modes, which tells you something about how confident Google is in it. Start a Magic Capture, point it at what’s happening, and when you’re done recording, Gemini will do some processing and pull out what it considers the best photos and video clips from the session.

During the Made by Google keynote last week, Google demoed the feature by recording some people shooting hoops on a basketball court. In the demonstration, Google said you could simply hold your phone and let it record while you take in the moment with your eyes. I have tried this exact scenario quite a few times, and let me tell you, it is extremely difficult to keep your subject in frame if you’re not staring at your screen. Magic Capture did a great job of pulling relevant images and clips from my recordings when I was making sure to keep my subject in frame by, you know, staring at my screen, but unless you have your phone mounted on a tripod or something, it’s naive to think you can ignore your phone completely.

That caveat aside, I really like this feature. I take a lot of videos on my phone, but I’m much more likely to revisit pictures. With Magic Capture, I can have both. The main caveat seems to be that stabilization isn’t as good on the clips it cuts compared to clips you’d take in video mode. Even so, I think Magic Capture will be useful for parents trying to capture moments of their kids, without needing to work so hard to get the perfect smile for a photo. Instead of marketing this feature as something that lets you be in the moment by not looking at your phone at all, it would probably be better to pitch it as something that will automatically grab great photos and short video clips for you, and all you need to do is point your phone and hit record.

Previous Next































1 / 17 Minimal Camera Look

While Magic Capture took most of the spotlight in Google’s keynote, maybe the most discussed photo upgrade this year is Camera Looks. I did a whole interview with Google’s camera chief about this feature going deep into how the new system was made, and there’s a lot of potential in the execution. Camera Looks is a new photography feature you can think of similar to Fujifilm’s film simulations, which let its cameras emulate different film styles on the JPGs they put out. On the Pixel 11 series, there are four modifications of the standard camera, with Original, Natural, Shadows, and Vanilla giving subtle tweaks to your image. But if you want to get more out there, there are six additional creative looks, called Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal.

Each of the looks can be modified to your liking, with adjustable settings like contrast, highlights, shadows, vibrance, tint, warmth, sharpness, and grain. What makes this a really interesting feature to me is that Google is adjusting the amount of computational processing it’s doing at capture, based on the settings you choose; it’s not just applying filters later. For example, the Digi mode will do less frame stacking and the Minimal mode will apply less sharpness and contrast.

Previous Next















1 / 9 Original Look

I really dig the looks, even right out of the box. They span from basic edits to quite inspired, and if you’re looking for something that gives you the “film simulation look” straight out of camera, these definitely deliver. It was high time Google added some more creative looks to the Pixel, especially considering it doesn’t have nearly as robust a third-party camera ecosystem as the iPhone. I’ve personally made the Minimal mode permanent on my phone for its unsharpened, minimally contrasty look, occasionally switching to Classic, but after testing them all, I think Velvet and Editorial will get a lot of use, since they have the most “film aesthetic” of the bunch. With less processed photos, you can actually see texture in photos, which is normally washed away by noise reduction algorithms.

Related The telephoto is the only phone camera that really matters

Overall camera quality on the Pixel 11 Pro series is great this year, and practically the only reason to pick up a Pro Pixel over the standard 11, aside from wanting a larger phone, in the case of the XL. The primary sensor is technically new, but Google tells me it’s the same size as last year and was swapped in because it uses slightly less power. The biggest camera hardware change is the new larger telephoto sensor, which Google says captures more light, and I can tell. Telephoto cameras are usually the weakest link in a smartphone’s camera arsenal, but even at 10x zoom, which is a 2x crop of the telephoto sensor, it was hard to notice any significant quality degradation. Plus, the transition between sensors is much smoother now, with only a very slight jump when switching between lenses.

The Camera Looks interface.

The Pixel 11 Pro also includes a 120x Pro Zoom mode, enabled by the new image signal processor in Tensor G6. Like the 100x Pro Zoom on the Pixel 10 Pro, Google is using generative AI to upscale your highly zoomed-in images to make them look more realistic. On objects without a lot of sharp edges this actually does a pretty good job, and Google will give you both the non-AI-enhanced and enhanced versions so you can see the difference.

I was in Spain during last week’s solar eclipse, and the Pixel 11 Pro did a good job of turning a zoomed-in photo of the moon from a blurry mess into something that looked good enough to elicit responses of awe when I posted it in Slack. But that was a relatively simple image, and shots with a lot more detail often look like an early AI-generated image, with skewed angles and edges, garbled text, and muddy tones. I’d only really use this if you needed to see information you can’t see with your normal eyes, not for artistic purposes.

100x ProRes Zoom 120x ProRes Zoom

The Pixel 11 Pro also gets a new, faster Night Sight, which Google says is about three times faster on average than the Pixel 10 Pro. In testing, most Night Sight images I took only needed to be held for one second, and I got all the same benefits you got from holding the phone for three or more seconds previously. This is the kind of quality-of-life update I love to see, and I’m glad Google is continuing to improve here.

I love Rambler, Magic Capture, and Camera Looks. If you’re looking to upgrade your phone this year, they’re legitimately great features. But after a week of use, it’s clear to me that the Pixel 11 Pro is not yet smart enough to help me use my phone less, despite what Google claims. Proactive Assistance is only bound to save you a few seconds and a few taps compared to just opening the apps and doing the steps yourself.

If you were hoping for the Pixel 11 Pro would help address your phone addiction, that’s probably not going to happen. But if you’re looking for a phone with the best voice-to-text on the market, great cameras with good built-in style, and solid hardware, the Pixel 11 Pro delivers.

Photography by David Imel / The Verge

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold feels like the end of an era
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The foldable phone market is in the middle of a huge transformation, but no one told Google.

Last year, Samsung transformed its Galaxy Z Fold 7 with a dramatically thinner design. This year, it made its phones thinner and lighter again, almost eliminated the crease, and introduced a new passport-sized form factor that feels like the future. Next month, Apple is expected to enter the market with a foldable iPhone that, rumor has it, includes all of the above and adds iOS too.

In the face of all that flux, Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold has hardly changed a thing.

Like the other Pixel 11 phones, this is an iterative hardware upgrade, but unlike the others its design feels dated already. It’s a little thinner and lighter than last year’s phone, the main camera is a bit better, the screens a touch brighter. But it’s mostly the same hardware, boosted by software updates like Camera Looks, multitasking Bubbles, and Creator Suite tools.

This isn’t a bad phone at all. The IP68 rating makes it tougher than Samsung’s latest, and the triple camera and solid software are both big draws. Perhaps not changing the design will even work in Google’s favor: The 11 Pro Fold’s aspect ratio sits in between the two extremes of Samsung’s 2026 lineup, its stocky Z Fold 8 and skinny Z Fold 8 Ultra, and despite a price hike still feels competitively priced with either.

That’s enough to mean the 11 Pro Fold still feels like a smart purchase right now, but I’m worried it won’t do for long.

At $1,899, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is $100 more than last year’s phone. Unlike on the other Pixel 11 models, that’s not masking a storage bump: This has the same 256GB starting storage as last year’s model. You can pay an extra $120 to get 512GB storage, and a further $230 to get 1TB. Every version comes with 16GB of RAM.

That $100 hike gets you a handful of hardware improvements on last year’s phone. The chipset has been upgraded to the new Tensor G6; both OLED displays run a bit brighter, now peaking at 3,600 nits; the 48-megapixel main camera uses a larger image sensor; and the Qi2 magnetic wireless charging now runs at 25W, up from 15W.

That’s just about it in terms of actual performance upgrades. There have been slightly bigger changes to the design though. This year’s phone is 0.7mm thinner when closed and weighs 19g less. That doesn’t sound like a whole lot, but holding the two generations side by side you can easily tell the difference, and the 11 Pro Fold is more comfortable to use for extended periods.

Still, it might be too little. Last year, Samsung slimmed its Z Fold 7 down dramatically, and pushed that even further this year, echoing similarly slim designs from Chinese rivals Oppo and Honor. Google’s foldable still feels big and bulky by comparison, like hardware that’s a generation behind.

The same is true of the display’s crease, which is pretty obvious even head-on, and easily noticeable when swiping from side to side. Oppo and Samsung have both worked miracles to make their creases almost invisible unless the light’s just right, and it feels like Google has a lot of catching up to do.

If you want a foldable that’s shaped like a regular phone when closed, this still fits the bill. Android 17’s Bubbles really come into their own on a foldable. The square inner screen made me miss the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

The almost square main display is well-suited to multitasking, helped by Bubbles, a new Android 17 feature that’s available on every Pixel but comes into its own on the foldables. Multiple apps can be opened in floating bubbles, allowing quick access to a smaller window that can be minimized just as easily. On the 11 Pro Fold’s larger display, those bubbles can float perpetually in a dedicated dock in the bottom-right corner for unobtrusive access. It’s ideal for hopping into Spotify to skip a song, diving into Todoist to tick off a task, or pulling up WhatsApp to reply to a message, all before getting back to whatever you were working on.

But in the wake of Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, this square screen feels a little behind the times. The industry seems to agree: Huawei has adopted the same design, Apple is expected to, and both Honor and Oppo are rumored to have wide foldables in the works. I enjoyed Samsung’s passport-sized form factor for its pocketability and natural feel when reading or watching TV and miss it while using this. By contrast, the 11 Pro Fold is tall when closed, and boxy when open. I do find it more comfortable than the unnaturally skinny Z Fold 8 Ultra though, and anyone split between Samsung’s two shapes may find this a happy medium.

Google says this new composite back material is much more durable than before. The 11 Pro Fold is Google’s thinnest foldable yet, but comfortably thicker than the competition.

Still, the 11 Pro Fold has its own advantages. Unlike those phones, it has an IP68 rating for dust- and water-resistance, following the similar score on the 10 Pro Fold. For a phone that can cost upwards of $2,000, that extra level of protection is worth more than mere peace of mind. Google also boasts that the new glass fiber composite back is three times more durable and “nearly impossible to crack.”

Google’s foldables remain the only ones to support Qi2 magnetic wireless charging, here upgraded to faster 25W speeds. The necessary magnets are part of why the phone is thicker than rivals, a tradeoff which will make sense for some.

This may have Qi2, but it doesn’t have a silicon-carbon battery, unlike Samsung’s new foldables. As a result, in slimming the phone, Google also shrunk the battery. The 4,806mAh capacity is only a little smaller than the 10 Pro Fold’s 5,015mAh though, and battery life itself has been fine, routinely lasting until the end of the day with a little bit to spare. This is still an all-day phone, it just isn’t especially close to being a two-day one.

This is HiLight — you won’t see it trigger very often I’m afraid. You get the same five color options for every contact, and that’s it.

The biggest design tweak is HiLight, Google’s attempt to reinvent the notification light by repurposing the camera flash into a multicolor LED. As a long-term notification light stan, I was excited to see Google resurrect it, but if this shambling corpse is the result, it should have stayed dead.

HiLight is currently only used for two things: a multicolor glow when you talk to Gemini, and a monocolor glow when one of your favorite contacts calls. Neither works unless the phone is lying flat and face-down with the screen off, and customization is limited to a measly pool of five colors for call alerts. Support for message notifications is coming later, Google says, with no word on whether it will ever be usable for notifications at large, serve as a charging indicator, or offer deeper customizability. If HiLight was going to be this basic, why did Google even bother?

More worthwhile is the single camera upgrade. The new 48-megapixel main camera sensor is the same as on the regular Pixel 11, and the two phones share matching 5x telephoto lenses too, with similar (though not identical) ultrawide and selfie cameras. Broadly speaking, the 11 Pro Fold camera is about the same as the 11’s and — on paper, at least — a step down from the Pro phones’.

Previous Next



































1 / 19 The larger main camera is the only change from last year’s 10 Pro Fold.

I’ve enjoyed shooting with this camera, especially on the main and telephoto lenses (the ultrawide shows its limits more, in both dynamic range and detail). The main sensor is big enough to deliver solid results even in dim lighting, helped by Google’s typically capable processing. The 5x telephoto is crisp at a distance, though fuzzy when pushed anywhere near its 30x maximum. Google hasn’t confirmed the telephoto’s minimum focus distance, but it feels like a few feet or so. Combined with the smallish sensor, which doesn’t deliver the natural bokeh of larger periscope sensors, this isn’t a great lens for closeups; instead the inferior ultrawide camera handles macro photography here. Still, with Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 dropping the telephoto entirely, having any third lens here — and a pretty good one, at that — is now a big boon for the Pixel foldable.

Google has bolstered the camera app with a whole suite of software upgrades, which might matter more than the hardware changes. I won’t go into them in too much detail here, since my colleague David Imel does a great job of exactly that in his Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL review, but I’ll give you the gist.

New Camera Looks are the biggest tweak, similar to the Film Simulations popularized on Fujifilm cameras. There are four default looks, which subtly change the style of an image, and another six with more dramatic effects, and each can be further tweaked with direct control over contrast, vibrance, sharpness, and more. These aren’t simply post hoc filters — they change processing at the moment of capture, and so have a tangible effect on the information the camera captures.

Previous Next















1 / 9 The default four Looks can be subtle. This is on the phone’s standard settings.

Also new is Magic Capture, a clever camera mode that records video and uses AI to pick out the best frames, giving you a video clip and photos without having to think about both. It’s a great option when you just want to capture kids and pets in action, and aren’t too stressed about lining up a perfect shot. Then there’s the Creator Suite, a set of tools specifically designed for content creators, including an onscreen teleprompter and the option to save videos and photos directly into project folders for easier organization.

Previous Next



1 / 3 Magic Capture grabbed these three shots of my cat Loaf from a 30-second video I took.

Software improvements elsewhere are focused on AI. Rambler is a dictation tool capable of interpreting meandering monologues and creating concise summaries instead. The bigger addition is Proactive Assistance, an upgraded version of Magic Cue that pops up with prompts for tasks it can help with. When it works, that is; the feature isn’t available in the UK at all, so I haven’t been able to test it, and my US-based colleagues reviewing the other Pixel 11 models found it hard to reliably trigger.

With Samsung rejigging its foldable lineup, and Apple’s first foldable iPhone seemingly imminent, Google might have picked the wrong year to be iterative. I wrote in my review that Samsung’s wider Z Fold 8 feels like the future of foldables; by extension, this might be the past.

The 11 Pro Fold is far from obsolete though. This is still, for now at least, this year’s only foldable with an IP68 rating and magnetic charging. Including a triple rear camera at the same price Samsung offers a double is a major selling point, and the suite of software updates — especially Camera Looks and Bubbles — might draw me back to this phone over either recent Galaxy. Whether they’re enough to compete with whatever Apple is about to offer is another question entirely.

Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you must agree to: Google Terms of Service

Google Play Terms of Service

Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS

Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.” There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services

“Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.”

Send usage and diagnostic data to Google

Let contacts nearby find and share with you Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: four mandatory agreements and at least seven optional agreements.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel Watch 5 is promising — but it isn’t finished
Tech.content:
The Google Pixel Watch 5 has, in many ways, been the hardest Pixel Watch to accurately review. Barely anything has changed in terms of hardware. The sizes are the same, the chips and battery got an itty-bitty boost, and there’s a new pyrite satin case finish. Instead, the big updates are all software-related: This year’s watch gets ambitious new health features that expand on the overhauled Google Health app and its AI coach introduced with the Fitbit Air earlier this year.

The only problem is those health updates aren’t here. The watch’s most interesting new features — blood pressure and insulin resistance trends, nightly sleep breathing quality, and strength training cues from the wrist — won’t start rolling out until next month. And in the case of breathing emergency detection, which calls emergency services if the device detects you’ve stopped breathing, the feature is still pending FDA clearance. (Europe will get it at launch, but this isn’t the sort of feature you can test anyway.)

That leaves me and the Pixel Watch 5 on my wrist in a bit of a reviewer’s pickle. All those features sound smart to me, but I can’t weigh in on whether they’re worth $399.99 — a $50 price hike over last year’s model — until they’re available. Given that half of those new metrics are meant to be viewed monthly, it’ll be a hot minute before I can write about them.

Which leaves the rest of the Pixel Watch 5 software updates: Wear OS 7, offline Gemini, a more accurate Raise to Talk feature, Proactive Assistance, more integrated gesture controls in the UI, AI watchfaces, some improved bedtime automations, and better GPS maps for outdoor activities. Broadly, I get the vibe Google’s going for — subtly helpful AI that enables glanceable, quickly actionable information — and I like it. However, except for GPS, these are refinements. They’re not mind-blowing updates that warrant morphing into the “Shut up and take my money!” meme. At launch, these will be exclusive to the Pixel Watch 5, but Google does have a history of software updates trickling down to older models with time.

Wear OS 7 isn’t a major departure from Wear OS 6. The double pinch and wrist turn gestures are now more directly integrated into the UI. At certain points (e.g., scrolling or selecting), you’ll see an animated chip of the pinching gesture. It’s a handy way of teaching you when a gesture can be used. During “live” activities — say, a workout or timer — another chip will appear on the main watchface. Flipping your wrist will dismiss your current screen or a call. These aren’t unique ideas. The Apple Watch has had them for a while. However, I love that they’re more prominently featured on the Pixel Watch (and not just the Watch 5). You’ll never see me pooh-pooh well-executed gesture controls on smartwatches simply because they’re not 100 percent new.

You’ll see this gesture chip appear more frequently in the Wear OS 7 UI. Raise to talk has been improved. Excuse this… sad brown tabby cat inspired AI watchface. Setting timers, launching apps, starting workouts, and opening your calendar are some things offline Gemini can do on the wrist. You’ll also see chips for live activities on the main watchface.

I was less enamored with Proactive Assistance. As my colleagues Dom Preston, David Imel, and Cameron Faulkner have noted in their Pixel 11 reviews, these Gemini-powered suggestions don’t always work as intended. You may also never notice them! On the watch, it was helpful when a friend texted me via Google Messages about my availability for plans. A chip for my Google Calendar instantly popped up. Except those were orchestrated scenarios for testing. In real life, I mostly plan hangouts over Slack or phone calls, where Gemini isn’t integrated. I get the concept, and I can see this improving with future updates. But for now your mileage will vary.

Offline Gemini was more convenient in testing than I’d anticipated. I had zero intention of running with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold that I’d paired with my Watch 5. I’ve dropped way too many a smartphone to risk wrecking a caseless, $1,900 phone. Nevertheless, Gemini was able to start a workout via voice command, as well as quickly obtain a GPS signal well out of Bluetooth range of the phone, and therefore internet. (I did this exact testing scenario before setting up cellular.) There’s still some latency when you use wrist-based Gemini — offline or otherwise — but not so egregious that it’s unusable. Especially for basic tasks.

Speaking of GPS, I called Google bold when it claimed the GPS on the Pixel Watch 5 outperforms that on the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro. It does this by utilizing 3D models of buildings, weather data, dual-frequency GPS, and other sensor signals to “correct” wonky GPS data after an activity. When I poked and prodded Google’s Pixel Watch reps at my demos, they didn’t flinch. There was no hedging, no caveats. Just a “we tested it in Manhattan, a GPS nightmare, go forth, Vee, and run till your little legs give out” kind of confidence. I still have a lot more GPS testing I want to do (different terrains, durations, and outdoor exercises), but I have to say — the GPS is dramatically improved, and it outperformed the Ultra 3 in my testing.

To test the GPS, I recorded three separate 20-to-30-minute walks in the West Village in Manhattan. During each of these walks, I walked in zigzags, annoyed cabbies by jaywalking across streets I wasn’t supposed to, and annoyed a friend by walking literal circles around her. As you can see in the screenshots here, the Ultra 3 overcorrected, so it appears like I’m mostly walking in a straight line. The Pixel Watch 5 didn’t catch all of my tests — but it did accurately register some of my zigzags, instances where I doubled back on purpose, and one time where I circled my friend. (I currently don’t have a Garmin Fenix 8 Pro, so I wasn’t able to compare it to that device, though you can check out DC Rainmaker’s more hardcore Pixel Watch 5 GPS tests here.)

Previous Next









1 / 6 In this loop, you can see how I’ve stuck to these West Village sidewalks, but the squiggles account for me walking around other pedestrians.

I doubt most Garmin or Ultra 3 fans will be enticed to switch based on improved GPS alone. I mean, the Pixel Watch’s design still doesn’t scream rugged durability — something most outdoor enthusiasts like. This is more Google leaning into its strengths to deliver a clever solution to a long-standing problem with Pixel and Fitbit wearables. I wouldn’t say it’s perfect. No GPS tracking is. It’s more that GPS accuracy is no longer a reason to hold back from getting a Pixel Watch if you want one.

Which leaves me to regale you with the most bizarre feature I tested: AI watchfaces.

I get why Google made this feature. It acknowledges that there’s a contingent of smartwatch fans who want as many watchfaces as possible and don’t want to rely on a company’s artistic curation. (Cough, Apple.) Theoretically, prompting an AI to generate a watchface of your specific idea makes sense.

But this is also AI. See: this incredibly dooftastic AI-generated watchface of a manta ray. This is not a manta ray. This is number-shaped blobs with eyes and cartoony dinosaur fins.

Pray tell, in what world is THIS a manta ray? It’s cute! It’s just not a manta ray!

I had more success asking for a cute Kirby-inspired watchface with “a playful font in a pink and purple theme.” Is it a tad unsettling that these are, again, Kirby-shaped numbers and Kirby’s face plastered onto them? Yeah, but it works. I had the most success with a cross-stitch-themed watchface featuring “fat and cute forest creatures and a retro font.” Sure, portions of the numbers are an embroidered satin stitch and not cross-stitches, but the spirit is there. My main gripe is how limited the customization is. You can tweak the appearance of the clock numbers, colors, and font, and choose one of three basic layouts, but little else. Is this a feature worth boiling oceans for? No, but it’s whimsical enough to please the people it’s intended for.

The hardware tweaks this year aren’t that noticeable. Swiping through screens is snappy but not radically improved. Like its predecessor, the 45mm Watch 5 lasted roughly 36 to 40 hours on a single charge in testing. A year later, I still like the watch stand charger. Fast charging is good enough that you can stick it on the charger while you shower and make it through the day (or night).

This prompt was not a keeper.

Right now, I feel comfortable saying the Pixel Watch 5 is a great Android smartwatch. RIP OnePlus, and Samsung has been coasting since the Galaxy Watch 6. So, like last year, this is the Android smartwatch to beat. It’s the one I’d recommend to Android smartwatch newcomers, and the $50 price hike thanks to RAMageddon isn’t as bad as it could’ve been.

If you’re an owner of a recent Pixel Watch, I don’t think this is the year to upgrade, though. And even if you’ve got a Pixel Watch 2 or earlier, I’d still wait until the new health features are out and tested before buying. Alternatively, you could opt for doubling up with a Fitbit Air instead of a new watch if you’re mainly annoyed about having to charge frequently for sleep tracking.

I don’t love feeling like a review is unfinished, but alas — that’s how it is this year. See you back in October for part two after the rest of the health features drop.

Photography by Victoria Song / The Verge

Agree to Continue: Google Pixel Watch 5 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Google Pixel Watch 5, you must pair it with an Android smartphone. That includes the phone’s Terms of Service, privacy policy, and any other permissions you grant, such as Bluetooth access and location services.
